item.title: Chest: Population-based Prevalence of Bronchiectasis in the United States
item.description:
Background: Bronchiectasis is a chronic, heterogeneous lung disease of rising prevalence; however, contemporary epidemiological data are lacking. Furthermore, paediatric prevalence and cystic fibrosis (CF)-related bronchiectasis prevalence are frequently absent from existing literature.

Research question: What is the prevalence of bronchiectasis in the United States?

Study design and methods: This retrospective, observational study utilised data from the Optum® Clinformatics® Data Mart claims database to estimate the age- and sex-standardised prevalence of bronchiectasis in the US in people of all ages and paediatrics (aged <18 years). Prevalence was stratified by age, sex, ethnicity and insurance coverage. Individuals were required to have ≥1 day of enrolment during the index period (2018-2022); the index date was the latest day in this period with ≥365 days of prior continuous enrolment.

Results: In the overall population, 94,392 cases of bronchiectasis were identified (median age, 76 years). Five-year prevalence was 221.6 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 220.1-223.1) per 100,000 persons and increased with age. Prevalence was higher among females (274.6 per 100,000 persons), Asians (302.3 per 100,000 persons) and Medicare Advantage enrolees (528.6 per 100,000 persons). In total, 1.4% of the overall population had a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. Five-year prevalence in the paediatric population (including 465 cases; median age, 12 years) was 11.9 (95% CI: 10.8-13.1) per 100,000 persons. Paediatric prevalence was similar between sexes, higher in Caucasians and higher in those with non-CF-related bronchiectasis than CF-related bronchiectasis.

Interpretation: This current study reports that bronchiectasis prevalence continues to increase in the US compared with previous studies, with a consistently higher prevalence in females and Asians, and that a lower proportion of individuals have CF-related bronchiectasis compared with non-CF-related bronchiectasis.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Awake intubation in a Japanese tertiary emergency department: a single-center retrospective descriptive study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Evidence on awake intubation in emergency departments (EDs) is limited. We aimed to describe patient characteristics, intubation indications, procedural practices, and outcomes for awake intubation in the ED.

Methods: This single-center retrospective descriptive study included consecutive adult patients who underwent tracheal intubation at a tertiary ED in Japan from April 2020 through December 2025. Patients intubated during cardiac arrest were excluded. Operational definition for awake tracheal intubation required topical upper airway anesthesia, no neuromuscular blockers before or during the initial attempt, and documented preservation of consciousness and spontaneous ventilation throughout that attempt. Outcomes included first-pass success, adverse events related to airway management, and definitive airway management, including rescue.

Results: Eighty-four patients underwent awake tracheal intubation, representing 5.5% of intubations in patients without cardiac arrest (84/1531). Upper airway infectious diseases were present in 54 patients (64.3%); airway-related indications accounted for 63 cases (75.0%). Emergency physicians performed 79 initial attempts (94.0%); a flexible bronchoscope was used initially in 49 patients (58.3%). First-pass success occurred in 63 patients (75.0%; 95% confidence interval, 64.4%-83.8%). Seven patients (8.3%) experienced adverse events related to airway management. Eighty patients (95.2%) achieved definitive airway management without a surgical airway. Four patients (4.8%) required a surgical airway, all after first-pass failure.

Conclusions: Awake intubation, performed primarily by emergency physicians, was used to manage upper airway infectious diseases with actual or impending obstruction in a tertiary ED. A flexible bronchoscope was used initially in over half of cases and most patients were intubated without a surgical airway.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Affect-laden momentary classes are associated with self-efficacy and substance use during early recovery from addiction
item.description:
Background: Affect is dynamic. During addiction recovery, it may be laden with experiences like pain or craving, which may combine to heighten risk for substance use. Multidimensional affect-laden experiences can be identified using a novel application of latent class analysis (LCA) applied to intensive longitudinal data. Identifying momentary affect-laden classes may enable detection of risk for substance use in adults in early addiction recovery.

Methods: Participants were adults (n = 185; M = 43.6, SD = 10.7; 40% female) who recently completed substance use disorder treatment. Every day for two weeks, they received five ecological momentary assessments of high- and low-arousal positive affect (PA) and negative affect (NA), boredom, tired, alert, pain, and craving. LCA was applied to these nine indicators of momentary affect. Same-moment self-efficacy for remaining abstinent and using substances by the next prompt were modeled as a function of momentary affect-laden classes.

Results: Six momentary affect-laden classes were identified: Activated Positive Affect (32% of all moments); Activated Negative Affect (13%); Low Energy (8%); Calm Positive Affect (26%); Pain, Craving, and Positive Affect (13%); and Pain, Craving, and Negative Affect (8%). Moments characterized by Pain and Craving had the poorest substance use outcomes. Low Energy moments were among the best in terms of self-efficacy and reduced risk for substance use. Activated Positive Affect moments were among the lowest risk for substance use, even compared to Calm Positive Affect moments.

Conclusions: Findings provide insight into detecting poor self-efficacy and subsequent substance use based on multidimensional affect-laden states during early recovery.

item.title: J Emerg Med: A Retrospective Review of Emergency Department Coronavirus 2019 Cases vs. County-Wide Cases to Demonstrate a Temporal Correlation
item.description:
Background: To better prepare for future Coronavirus 2019 (COVID-19) variants, new forms of surveillance are necessary to predict outbreaks and prepare communities and hospitals.

Objectives: We examined the temporal correlation between emergency department (ED) and county COVID-19 cases and determine if ED COVID-19 trends can serve as an indicator to predict county-level outbreaks.

Methods: A retrospective analysis of COVID-19 data from March 2020 to April 2023 was conducted, comparing hospital COVID-19 positive cases to local county positive cases. Data were analyzed using two metrics: a positivity cutoff and a cross-correlation analysis. We set the positivity cutoff (percent of positive tests to total tests) at 4% threshold based on guidelines from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and identified dates when ED and county positivity surpassed this threshold. The cross-correlation analysis between the county and the ED determined the time lag interval (in days) that had the strongest correlation between daily ED and county positive case volume per outbreak.

Results: There were both seven ED and county dates that met the positivity cutoff but only five that corresponded to the same outbreaks. The county outbreaks preceded ED outbreaks, ranging from 2 to 59 days, with a mean of 42 days prior. The cross-correlational analysis underwent an additional sensitivity analysis, resulting in an R-squared value ranging 0.8435-0.9271, averaging 8.25 days of county precedence.

Conclusion: ED data is not a suitable predictor of county-level COVID-19 cases; however, the strong correlation of county precedence can prove helpful to prepare hospitals for future outbreaks.

item.title: J Emerg Med: Sex and Age-Based Effect on Outcomes in the Setting of Traumatic Hemorrhage
item.description:
Background: Survival differences between injured females and males have been demonstrated.

Study objectives: To analyze trauma survival stratified by sex and age for a given transfusion volume.

Methods: The Trauma Quality Improvement Program registry was analyzed from 2020 to 2023. Patients ≥15 years who received any volume of blood products within 4 hours were included.

Results: There were 13,987 patients (3165/13,987, 22.6% female) who received 75-600 mL/kg of all blood products within the first 4 hours of admission, i.e., the range where a difference in cumulative 24-hour survival between males and females was observed. In this range, the cumulative probability of 24-hour survival was lower for females compared to males (46 vs. 51%, respectively). This difference was not observed in the adjusted analysis (odds ratio 0.93, 95% confidence interval 0.84-1.02). In the unadjusted age and sex subanalysis, females >50 years had the highest mortality of any of the four groups of patients once ∼100 mL/kg of blood products had been transfused. Both males and females aged 15-50 years had the lowest mortality for any volume of transfusion; males >50 years had intermediate mortality. In the regression analysis performed on patients who received a total volume of 100-600 mL/kg of transfusion, 15- to 50-year-old males had significantly lower 24-hour survival compared to similarly aged females. There was no difference in this parameter between the females and males who were >50 years.

Conclusion: Adjusting for differences did not reveal a difference in overall survival between males and females; younger males had lower survival compared to similarly aged females.

item.title: J Addict Med: The Relationship Between Overdose Experience and Social Functional Impairment in Individuals With a History of Substance Use
item.description:
Background: Substance-use disorders can profoundly affect nearly every aspect of an individual's life. The threat of drug overdoses, driven primarily by illicit fentanyl, remains a major public health crisis. Functional disability refers to limitations in performing everyday tasks and participating in life situations. We examined the association between overdose experiences (such as naloxone administration, medical intervention, unintentional fentanyl exposure, or recent overdoses) and functional disability, manifested in both social and family domains, in a population of individuals with a history of substance use.

Methods: Overdose experiences, functional disability, and sociodemographic factors were analyzed from selected survey instruments, including overdose Questionnaire, Sheehan Disability Survey, and Demographics Survey, administered as part of a battery of questionnaires in a prospective longitudinal multisite cohort study of individuals with severe mental health and substance-use disorders (ROAR CANADA). Impairment in social life and family responsibilities were examined in relation to various overdose experiences among individuals with substance-use disorder backgrounds.

Results: Female sex was the strongest and most consistent correlate of disability, with higher adjusted odds of greater social (OR=2.61: CI: 1.75, 3.89) and family disability (OR=2.47; CI: 1.65, 3.67). Unintentional fentanyl consumption was associated with greater social disability (OR=1.63; CI: 1.07, 2.48) and remained a stable predictor of markedly impaired social and family functioning across Elastic Net resampling analyses.

Conclusion: Among treatment-seeking individuals with severe concurrent mental health and substance-use disorders, greater functional disability was most consistently associated with female sex, while unintentional fentanyl exposure was associated with greater social disability. These cross-sectional findings identify clinically relevant correlates of impaired social and family functioning and support longitudinal research to clarify temporal relationships and evaluate targeted functional assessment and rehabilitation approaches.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Symptom Misrepresentation to Obtain Antibiotics
item.description:
Importance: Misrepresentation of symptoms, whether through exaggeration, omission, or fabrication, can represent an important barrier to effective patient-clinician communication and shared decision-making, including in the context of antibiotic treatment.

Objective: To examine the prevalence, reasons for, and characteristics associated with self-reported misrepresentation of symptoms to obtain antibiotics.

Design, setting, and participants: This survey study recruited a national, nonprobability sample of US adults to participate in an online survey from January 8 to February 13, 2026. Data were analyzed from February to March 18, 2026.

Main outcomes and measures: Outcomes of interest were 2 types of symptom misrepresentation (exaggeration and fabrication) to obtain antibiotics and the reasons underlying these behaviors. Additional questions measured antibiotic-related beliefs, experiences, and behaviors and demographics.

Results: Of 1371 eligible participants, the final sample included 959 individuals (mean [SD] age of 50.7 [17.6] years; 478 [49.8%] female). Overall, 268 respondents (27.9%) reported ever misrepresenting their symptoms to a clinician to get antibiotics. This included 108 respondents (40.3%) who exaggerated existing symptoms (eg, told their clinician they had a cough for 2 weeks when they only had it for 1 week), 19 respondents (7.1%) who fabricated symptoms (eg, told their clinician they had a fever when they did not), and 141 (52.6%) who did both. Cold-like symptoms (eg, cough, sore throat) were the most frequently misrepresented (176 respondents [65.7%]). The most commonly endorsed reasons for misrepresenting symptoms were illness severity, perceived antibiotic efficacy, returning to responsibilities, and desire for autonomy in their treatment decisions. Younger age (age 18-33 vs ≥65 years: odds ratio [OR], 3.20 [95% CI, 1.58-6.63]; age 34-55 vs ≥65 years: OR, 3.05 [95% CI, 1.55-6.17]), often feeling that clinicians do not take their symptoms seriously (OR, 2.19 [95% CI, 1.49-3.22]), believing that antibiotic resistance is a hoax (OR, 1.98 [95% CI, 1.34-2.93]), reporting more comorbidities (OR, 1.16 [95% CI, 1.05-1.28]), having higher lying-acceptability scores (OR, 1.49 [95% CI, 1.23-1.80]), and needing help reading health materials (OR, 2.40 [95% CI, 1.62-3.54]) were associated with higher odds of reporting symptom misrepresentation to obtain antibiotics. In contrast, dislike of taking antibiotics (OR, 0.89 [95% CI, 0.81-0.99]) and higher antibiotic knowledge (OR, 0.73 [95% CI, 0.58-0.91]) were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation.

Conclusions and relevance: In this survey study of US adults, nearly 30% of respondents reported misrepresenting symptoms to get antibiotics from a clinician, most commonly cold-like symptoms. Findings highlight the need for strategies to promote antibiotic knowledge and improve patient-clinician communication to address factors contributing to symptom misrepresentation.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Small Area Deprivation and Depression or Anxiety in a Nationwide Cohort
item.description:
Importance: Prior studies suggest increased risk of mental health conditions in deprived residential areas, but robust evidence leveraging nationwide health care and prescription registers, including primary care, with socioeconomic databases is lacking.

Objective: To examine the association between small-area deprivation and depression or anxiety in people aged 10 to 50 years without recent history of these conditions.

Design, setting, and participants: This nationwide register-based cohort study with sibling analysis was conducted in Sweden January 1, 2015, through December 31, 2023, with analysis completed in January to September 2026. Participants were registered in Sweden throughout the study period, including siblings with discordant-exposure status.

Exposure: Small-area deprivation in 2015 was defined for 5984 areas using an Index for Multiple Deprivation in Sweden categorized into quartiles.

Main outcomes and measures: Depression or anxiety was defined as the first diagnosis or the first prescription date if no diagnosis was recorded in the study period. Hazard ratios (HRs) for the outcome through December 31, 2023, were computed using Cox regression models adjusted for confounders. Sibling analyses used stratified Cox regression with robust error variance. We separately tested for interactions between small-area deprivation and age, sex, and urbanicity in the association with the outcome.

Results: A total of 4 065 375 participants (2 169 625 male [53.4%]; median [IQR] age, 30 [20-41] years), including 1 301 647 siblings, were included. Incidence rates per 1000 person-years for depression or anxiety varied across deprivation levels from 22.8 (95% CI, 22.7-22.9; very low) to 25.6 (95% CI, 25.5-25.7; very high). The HR for depression or anxiety associated with living in the most vs least deprived area was 1.18 (95% CI, 1.17-1.19) and 1.15 (95% CI, 1.13-1.17) in the sibling cohort. Urban (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.17-1.19) and periurban (HR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.18-1.23) residents in most vs least deprived areas had higher depression or anxiety rates than rural counterparts (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.08-1.14).

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, people in the most vs least deprived areas had increased depression or anxiety rates, and the association remained in sibling comparisons. There were increased rates of depression or anxiety associated with living in the most vs least deprived areas of urban and periurban settings compared with rural settings, potentially reflecting worse outcomes in deprived urban areas or less contact with mental health services in remote and rural areas.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Survival After Risk-Reducing Mastectomy in Patients With Pathogenic Variants in BRCA1 and BRCA2: A Network Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Importance: The independent survival benefit of risk-reducing mastectomy (RRM), separate from risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy (RRSO), remains uncertain among patients with pathogenic variants (PVs) in BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes.

Objective: To evaluate the association of RRM, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based screening, and mammography alone with all-cause and breast cancer-specific mortality using RRSO-adjusted estimates.

Data sources: MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 1990, to May 28, 2026. Search structures, subject headings, and keywords were tailored to each database.

Study selection: Inclusion criteria were English-language prospective and retrospective observational studies of adult female patients with PV or likely PV in BRCA1 and BRCA2 who underwent RRM or breast cancer screening (MRI-based with or without mammography, or mammography alone), with RRSO excluded by design or adjusted for in multivariable analysis. Studies including females with prior breast or ovarian cancer were excluded.

Data extraction and synthesis: Study reporting followed Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 network meta-analysis extension. Two authors independently performed study selection, data extraction, and bias assessment using a risk-of-bias assessment tool (ROBINS-I V2) and a grading approach (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation [GRADE]). Frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was performed with surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) estimation. Sensitivity analysis was conducted for the BRCA1 cohort.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcome was breast cancer-specific mortality. All outcomes were analyzed and reported as hazard ratios (HRs) with corresponding 95% CIs.

Results: Five observational studies with 7937 female patients (median [range] age, 35.9 [unreported] years to 43.4 [32.0-55.7] years) met the inclusion criteria. RRM was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with MRI-based screening (HR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.22-0.63) and mammography alone (HR, 0.16; 95% CI, 0.08-0.32). RRM was also associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality compared with mammography alone (HR, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.44) but did not have significantly lower mortality than MRI-based screening (HR, 0.26; 95% CI, 0.05-1.35). In BRCA1-only analyses, RRM was associated with lower breast cancer-specific mortality compared with MRI-based screening (HR, 0.13; 95% CI, 0.03-0.66) and mammography alone (HR, 0.03; 95% CI, 0.00-0.15). SUCRA rankings indicated RRM had the highest likelihood of association with the lowest all-cause mortality (SUCRA value, 99.9%). Risk of bias was critical for 4 studies, and certainty of evidence was rated as very low for all 5 studies.

Conclusions and relevance: In this systematic review and network meta-analysis of RRSO-adjusted analyses, RRM was associated with lower all-cause mortality compared with breast cancer screening among females with PVs in BRCA1 and BRCA2, with the greatest magnitude of association for breast cancer-specific mortality observed in BRCA1 PV carriers. These findings provide less confounded survival estimates to support individualized shared decision-making for RRM.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: AI-Generated Draft Response Tool, Message Turnaround Time, and After-Hours Replies Among Health Care Professionals
item.description:
Importance: Patient portal message volumes have increased, creating substantial administrative burden for clinicians and contributing to after-hours electronic health record work. The Epic In Basket Augmented Response Technology tool generates artificial intelligence-drafted replies to patient messages and has been widely deployed to reduce this burden, yet assessment of efficiency remains limited.

Objective: To examine the associations of response tool adoption, use, and habituation with message turnaround time and after-hours response.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study was conducted using clinician-level panel regression with individual fixed effects. All first responses to patient portal messages sent at Columbia University Irving Medical Center (CUIMC) between March 1, 2023, and May 15, 2025, were analyzed.

Exposure: Enterprise-level response tool deployment December 2024.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcomes were log-transformed message turnaround time, defined as the elapsed time between patient message submission and first response sent by a clinician, and whether the response was sent outside working hours.

Results: The analysis included 983 154 responses from 1542 clinicians (770 [49.9%] female) and 272 091 patients (mean [SD] age, 48.1 [21.6] years; 121 370 [44.6%] female) at CUIMC. Response tool adoption was associated with an 8.6% (95% CI, 4.6%-12.9%; P < .001) increase in overall message turnaround time. Using the tool was associated with a significant reduction in turnaround time (-29.5% [95% CI, -34.5% to -24.1%]; P < .001). Turnaround time findings were robust across sensitivity analyses. Response tool use was not associated with an overall reduction of after-hours messaging burden (0.61 [95% CI, -1.02 to 2.24] percentage points; P = .46). However, for test results-related queries received during working hours, response tool use was associated with a reduction in after-hours responses (-3.67 [95% CI, -6.94 to -0.39] percentage points; P = .03), and for all messages received after hours, response tool use was associated with an increase in after-hours responses (4.52 [95% CI, 1.54-7.50] percentage points; P = .003). These after-hours findings were sensitive to the definition of working hours in sensitivity analyses.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, response tool adoption was associated with increased turnaround time. Response tool use was associated with reduced turnaround time and with fewer after-hours responses for test results-related queries received during working hours, but more after-hours responses for messages received outside working hours. These findings suggest that the tool may reduce the barrier to responding to certain messages while not uniformly reducing burden.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Surgeon- and Practice-Directed Interventions to Reduce Overtreatment of Low-Risk Thyroid Cancer
item.description:
Importance: Overtreatment of low-risk thyroid cancer (LRTC) exists worldwide, with many patients unnecessarily undergoing total thyroidectomy. Effective surgeon- and practice-directed interventions to reduce overtreatment are needed.

Objective: To identify barriers to and facilitators of implementing surgeon- and practice-directed interventions aimed at reducing total thyroidectomy for LRTC.

Design, setting, and participants: This qualitative study, conducted between June 1, 2024, and February 28, 2025, used a focused ethnography that included semistructured interviews of 19 thyroid surgeons and site visits to 7 community and academic practices where thyroidectomy is performed.

Main outcomes and measures: Participants ranked 6 potential interventions for reducing overtreatment of LRTC and identified implementation barriers and facilitators. Verbatim transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis to identify the most acceptable aspects of the interventions. Ethnographic field notes provided context for interview results.

Results: The 19 participants were predominantly male (13 [68.4%]), with a mean (SD) age of 46.6 (8.2) years. Participants' opinions on the usefulness of the proposed interventions differed. However, when asked to explain their intervention rankings, participants' reasoning for why they preferred particular interventions followed similar patterns. These patterns led to 3 key themes for the development of an effective intervention: (1) thyroid cancer is complex (a one-size-fits-all approach would not allow for nuanced decision-making); (2) although participants recognized the value of an intervention, they believed interventions were not appropriate for their own practice; and (3) surgeon professional identity can impact practice change, resulting in either reluctance toward practice change or motivation to change. Barriers to implementation observed during site visits were associated with differences in the clinic environment (eg, completing clinical demands, physical infrastructure) and across staffing and staff interactions (eg, presence of trainees, patient-surgeon interactions).

Conclusions and relevance: In this qualitative study of thyroid surgeons, key factors were identified for the development of an intervention for reducing overtreatment of LRTC. Participants' assessment of proposed interventions indicated a successful intervention must be seen as useful, surgeons may be motivated through performance feedback, and the intervention must fit well into the existing surgical workflow. Results demonstrated that an acceptable and effective intervention in this setting may take many forms as long as the intervention considered both behavior change and the end user.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: National Institutes of Health Funding for Research About Transgender and Nonbinary Youths
item.description:
Importance: Research is needed to improve health and well-being for transgender and nonbinary (TGNB) youths (<18 years), including access to gender-affirming medical care (GAMC) and associated clinical outcomes. Investment in TGNB youth research at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has not been well-characterized even though it has been the source of considerable public debate and recent policy changes to restrict funding.

Objective: To examine patterns of funding for TGNB youth research at NIH, including trends over time, demographic subgroups, GAMC and other health topics, and geographic distribution.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study examined NIH funding for research related to TGNB youths from 2012 to 2024, using the NIH Research Portfolio Online Reporting Tools (RePORTER) database. Awards were included if abstracts explicitly focused on TGNB youth health. This study took place at the University of Minnesota and used publicly available data regarding domestic and international grants administered by NIH. It did not include participants.

Exposure: NIH funding for TGNB youth research.

Main outcomes and measures: The amount of TGNB youth awards, both as a total and a proportion of the NIH portfolio was calculated. Award characteristics (eg, administering institute) were extracted from NIH RePORTER, and costs were inflation-adjusted to 2024 dollar values. Systematic coding of abstracts characterized demographic subgroups and health topics for each award.

Results: Between 2012 and 2024, 97 awards and 42 supplements totaling $158.3 million were issued for research about TGNB youths, representing 0.06% of the NIH portfolio. Funding increased over the study period and was concentrated among institutions in states with currently protective GAMC policies. To align funding with estimates of the population size of TGNB youths, investment would need to increase by a factor of 3.5 to 9.8. Nonbinary youths and racially and ethnically minoritized TGNB youths were minimally funded. Common research topics included HIV or AIDS ($68.8 million; 43.5%) and mental health ($78.0 million; 49.3%), with the latter associated with increases in total funding from 2021 onward. GAMC funding ($38.3 million; 24.2%) increased moderately over time.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of NIH awards, research about TGNB youths increased from 2012 to 2024, but it was substantially below population-proportional levels, reflecting historical underfunding and structural barriers in research prioritization.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Physician Sex and Outcomes Among Hospitalized Patients
item.description:
Importance: Prior studies have shown that patients treated by female physicians experience better outcomes than those treated by male physicians, but evidence has often focused on surgical populations. The association between physician sex and outcomes among hospitalized medical patients across different health care systems remains less well understood.

Objective: To examine associations between physician sex and care outcomes among hospitalized medical patients admitted with common medical diagnoses in Ontario, Canada.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based, retrospective cohort study was conducted between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2022, among inpatients aged 18 years or older admitted with 1 of 7 common acute medical conditions in Ontario, Canada. Data were analyzed from August 16, 2024, to July 13, 2026.

Exposure: Physician sex, defined in 2 ways: binary sex of the most responsible physician during hospital admission and proportion of in-hospital days managed by a female physician.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes were 30-day mortality and hospital readmission. Secondary outcomes included 90-day and 1-year mortality and readmission and index hospital length of stay. Multivariable generalized estimating equations were used to calculate adjusted odds ratios (AORs) accounting for patient-, physician-, and hospital-level covariates.

item.description:
Importance: Perceived racial discrimination has been shown to be associated with lower medication adherence and poorer health outcomes among Black patients. Individuals perceive discrimination when they (1) observe negative behaviors and (2) attribute these behaviors to racial bias; effectively reducing racial discrimination, therefore, entails limiting actions that patients most readily attribute to bias.

Objective: To examine behaviors associated with Black patients' attribution of negative behaviors by health care workers to racial discrimination.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional survey study was conducted at 15 health-oriented events in Minneapolis and St Paul, Minnesota, in 2025. A convenience sample of non-Hispanic Black adults older than 40 years was recruited. Participants who experienced negative behaviors by health care workers were included.

Exposures: Self-reported experiences of 10 negative behaviors and level of trust in the health care system.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was attribution of negative behaviors to racial discrimination (ARD). Logistic regressions were used to examine associations between experiencing individual behaviors, sum of negative behaviors, and trust in the health care system with ARD.

Results: A total of 284 adults were recruited, and 152 who experienced negative behaviors were included. Six observations were removed owing to missing data on patients' attribution for these behaviors, resulting in a final analytic sample of 146 participants (mean [SD] age, 58.7 [10.9] years; 116 female [79.5%]); 109 participants (74.7%) attributed negative behaviors to racial bias. Greater exposure to negative behaviors was associated with higher odds of ARD (odds ratio [OR], 1.42; 95% CI, 1.14-1.76). Having concerns dismissed (OR, 3.49; 95% CI, 1.57-7.79), being spoken to in a cold or impersonal manner (OR, 5.04; 95% CI, 1.82-13.90), and being stereotyped (OR, 4.22; 95% CI, 1.63-10.93) were directly associated with ARD. Trust in the health care system was not significantly associated with ARD (OR, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.46-1.04). In a multivariable analysis, total negative behaviors remained associated with ARD (OR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.12-1.73), and trust did not.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of communication behaviors attributed to racial discrimination, experiencing dismissiveness, relational coldness, and stereotyping were associated with Black patients' attribution of negative behaviors to racial bias. Interventions targeting these behaviors may reduce patients' experience of health care discrimination.

item.title: Prehosp Emerg Care: Prevalence of Persistent Severe Hypertension and Rates of Treatment Among Pregnant Patients in the Prehospital Setting
item.description:
Objectives: Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) contribute to maternal and fetal morbidity and mortality and require time-sensitive intervention. In April 2025, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), in collaboration with the National Association of EMS Physicians (NAEMSP) and the National Association of EMTs (NAEMT), published new guidelines on the prehospital management of elevated blood pressure in pregnancy. The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence of persistent severe hypertension among pregnant patients encountered by prehospital clinicians, characterize baseline frequency of pre-guideline treatment, and establish a benchmark to inform implementation of these guidelines.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational cohort study using the 2024 ESO Data Collaborative public release research dataset (January 1 to December 31, 2024). We identified all 9-1-1 ground EMS scene responses for patients documented as pregnant beyond 20 weeks of gestation. We excluded injury-related encounters and patients outside the World Health Organization-defined childbearing age range (15 to 49 years). Consistent with the new guidelines, we defined persistent severe hypertension as at least two documented blood pressure measurements with systolic blood pressure ≥ 160 mmHg or diastolic blood pressure ≥ 110 mmHg. We defined guideline-adherent treatment as administration of both magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) and an antihypertensive medication (labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine).

Results: We identified 39,546 eligible 9-1-1 ground EMS scene responses for patients beyond 20 weeks of gestation. The prevalence of persistent severe hypertension was 3.1% (n = 1,234/39,546). Among these patients, 77 (6.2%) received magnesium sulfate only, 19 (1.5%) received an antihypertensive medication only, and 10 (0.8%) received guideline-adherent treatment with both magnesium sulfate and an antihypertensive medication.

Conclusions: Approximately 1 in 32 pregnant patients beyond 20 weeks of gestation encountered by prehospital clinicians had persistent severe hypertension. In the year prior to dissemination of the 2025 ACOG, NAEMSP, and NAEMT-supported guidelines, fewer than 1% received guideline-adherent treatment with both magnesium sulfate and an antihypertensive medication. These findings establish a national benchmark and identify opportunities to improve prehospital care through protocol development, medication availability, clinician education, and implementation of updated guidelines.

Rationale: Self-directed lifestyle interventions may improve access to weight loss care in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), but effectiveness in routine practice is unknown.

Objective: Test whether a proactively delivered self-directed lifestyle intervention improves weight and sleep-related quality of life versus usual care.

Methods: POWER enrolled patients with OSA and body mass index of 30-45 kg/m2, recruited from Veteran Affairs (VA) sites nationwide, and randomized participants to a self-directed intervention based on the Diabetes Prevention Program with video-based sessions, readings, and regular coaching reminders or usual care. item.title: J Am Coll Emerg Physicians Open: Predictors of Blood Culture Ordering and Results for Febrile Infants Aged 91 to 365 Days in the Emergency Department
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Introduction: The risk of invasive bacterial infections has dropped significantly among febrile infants due to widespread vaccination efforts. In older infants (age 91 days and older), diagnostic guidance is limited, and blood culture ordering is based on clinical judgment. We sought to evaluate blood culture ordering practice, bacteremia incidence, and the patient characteristics of true positive blood culture results.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of febrile pediatric patients aged 91 to 365 days who presented to Kaiser Permanente Northern California emergency departments (EDs) between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2019, who had blood cultures drawn. We identified variables related to blood culture ordering using a generalized linear mixed model and adjudicated all positive results to determine rates of true bacteremia or contamination, as well as clinical characteristics of children with true positive bacteremia.

Results: Among 5543 febrile infants, 611 (11.0%) underwent blood culture testing. After adjustment for covariates, higher ED temperature (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 1.40, 95% CI, 1.30 to 1.50), presence of comorbidities (aOR 2.55, 95% CI, 2.00 to 3.25), and younger age (aOR 0.996, 95% CI, 0.995 to 0.998, P < .001) were associated with blood culture ordering. Of the 37 (6.1%) positive blood cultures, only 16 (2.6%) were true positives. All true positives occurred in infants with either an identifiable risk factor or a clinically evident source of infection. There were no cases of occult bacteremia identified.

Conclusion: In febrile infants aged 91 to 365 days, true bacteremia was rare and associated with significant comorbidities or an obvious infectious source. Our findings suggest a more directed approach to ED blood culture ordering.

item.title: J Am Coll Emerg Physicians Open: Remimazolam for Procedural Sedation During Synchronized Electrical Cardioversion in the Emergency Department
item.category: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
item.description:
Synchronized electrical cardioversion necessitates procedural sedation to ensure patient comfort and amnesia. Remimazolam is a novel, ultrashort-acting intravenous benzodiazepine with organ-independent esterase metabolism, a favorable safety profile, and flumazenil reversibility. Although, previously described in the electrophysiology laboratory, use of remimazolam has not been reported for electrical cardioversion in the emergency department. In this case, a 67-year-old man with sudden-onset paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented in symptomatic atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response. Following rate and rhythm optimization, the decision was made to proceed with synchronized electrical cardioversion under procedural sedation. After consent was obtained, remimazolam (5 mg intravenously) was administered as a single bolus. Sedation onset occurred at 49 seconds, with adequate depth achieved at 1 minute 37 seconds. A single synchronized biphasic 200 joule electric shock was successfully delivered at 2 minutes 20 seconds, converting the patient to normal sinus rhythm. Eye opening occurred at 3 minutes 50 seconds, with return to baseline orientation at 4 minutes 30 seconds. No apnea, hypoxia, hemodynamic instability, or procedural recall was observed. Continuous end-tidal carbon dioxide monitoring confirmed uninterrupted spontaneous ventilation throughout. The rapid onset, hemodynamic stability, and remarkably brief recovery time observed support its potential as a first-line sedative for emergency department cardioversion. Further prospective study in this setting is warranted.

Rationale: Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the accepted first-line treatment for insomnia, but its scalability and safety in patients with co-morbid insomnia and obstructive sleep apnea (COMISA) remain unclear. Clinician-guided digital CBT-I (D-CBT-I) is a potential treatment option that may address these limitations in COMISA.

Objective: To evaluate the effectiveness of clinician-guided D-CBT-I versus sleep hygiene education (SHE) in patients with COMISA.

Methods: This randomized trial (n = 88) compared clinician-guided D-CBT-I (6 weekly online sessions: sleep restriction, sleep hygiene, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, relapse prevention) with SHE alone. Blinded outcome assessments were conducted at baseline, posttreatment (6 weeks), and 3-month follow-up. Primary outcomes were Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scores at posttreatment and 3-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included daytime sleepiness, sleep parameters, OSA severity, neurocognitive function, and adverse events.

Measurements and main results: At 3-month follow-up, intention-to-treat analysis showed significantly greater improvements with D-CBT-I versus SHE on ISI (-9.5 vs. -4.0 points; d = -1.18, P = 0.001) and PSQI (-4.9 vs. -1.8 points; d = -0.87, P = 0.001); D-CBT-I also reduced subjective sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale; -3.4 vs. -1.0 points; d = -0.68, P < 0.001). Conclusion: Clinician-guided D-CBT-I improved insomnia and OSA severity, and enhanced cognitive function in COMISA patients.

item.title: Crit Care: Chlorhexidine within a standardized oral-care bundle for the prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia: a pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover trial in six medical intensive care units
item.description:
Background: Chlorhexidine (CHX) has been a long-standing component of oral-care bundles for preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), but recent evidence has questioned its benefit in non-cardiac-surgery ICU. We evaluated whether adding 0.12% CHX to standardized oral-care bundle provides incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU.

Methods: We conducted a prospective, pragmatic cluster-randomized crossover (AB/BA) trial in six adult medical ICUs of a single tertiary-care academic hospital in Bhubaneswar, India. ICUs were randomized as three ICUs of two Period of 9 months with the multicomponent oral-care bundle without chlorhexidine and three with the same bundle plus 0.12% chlorhexidine with a 1-month wash-in and re-training interval. Consecutive adults ventilated for ≥ 48 h were included. The primary outcome was VAP incidence density (Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score (CPIS) > 6) as per 1,000 ventilator-days. Secondary outcomes were 28-day all-cause mortality, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU length of stay, 28- day ventilator-free days, Beck Oral Assessment Scale (BOAS) and Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) scores. The primary model was a population-averaged Poisson generalized estimating equation (GEE) and adjustment for treatment, period, sequence, age, sex, APACHE II, and SOFA.

Results: A total of 1,035 patients (637 No CHX, 398 CHX) accrued 10,024 ventilator-days (5,918 vs. 4,106). Groups were well balanced at baseline (mean age ≈ 55 years; APACHE II ≈ 19.6; SOFA ≈ 13.4). VAP occurred in 100/5,918 ventilator-days (16.9 per 1,000) vs. 77/4,106 (18.8 per 1,000) (No CHX vs. CHX). The adjusted Poisson incidence rate ratio was 1.08 (95% CI 0.84-1.38; p = 0.56). 28-day mortality was 28.7% vs. 26.4% (no CHX vs. CHX) (adjusted OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65-1.15; p = 0.33). ICU length of stay was longer in the CHX arm (adjusted mean difference + 0.89 days, 95% CI + 0.19 to + 1.58; p = 0.013). BOAS and CPOT scores did not differ.

Conclusions: In this trial, adding 0.12% chlorhexidine to a standardized oral-care bundle did not reduce VAP incidence density or 28-day mortality and was associated with a modest increase in ICU length of stay. Routine CHX use provided no clear incremental benefit in a mixed medical ICU population.

item.title: Resuscitation: Artificial Intelligence-Assisted, Electrocardiogram-Derived, Sequential Rule-Based Decision Tree for Exclusion of Acute Coronary Syndrome as the Etiology of Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study
item.description:
Background: After out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) with return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC), deciding which patients without ST-segment elevation warrant emergency coronary angiography is difficult, as standard electrocardiogram (ECG), troponin, and echocardiography are limited in the early post-arrest window. We aimed to develop a sequential rule-based decision tree to identify post-ROSC patients in whom acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is unlikely to be the arrest etiology.

Methods: In this single-center retrospective study, adult patients with OHCA were divided into development (2020-2024; n=329) and temporal validation (2025; n=71) cohorts. Post-ROSC 12-lead ECGs were analyzed by a deep-learning platform generating ten digital biomarkers. Five candidate biomarkers were combined into a rhythm-stratified sequential decision tree under a zero false-negative constraint; its performance was compared with that of individual biomarkers and validated in the temporal cohort.

Results: The tree classified 171/329 (52.0%) and 32/71 (45.1%) patients in the development and validation cohorts, respectively, as "ACS not likely," with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified at any node. Yield concentrated in the non-shockable subgroup, in which the model excluded 169/261 (64.8%) non-ACS cases (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC], 0.824), outperforming each individual biomarker. In the shockable subgroup, which carries a high pretest probability of ACS, 38/40 patients (95.0%) were retained as "ACS not excluded."

Conclusions: A rhythm-stratified, rule-based decision tree combining AI-assisted ECG-derived biomarkers classified approximately half of post-OHCA patients as "ACS not likely" with no adjudicated ACS case misclassified, principally in the non-shockable subgroup. This transparent, bedside-deployable framework warrants prospective multicenter evaluation.

item.description:
Background: Recurrent cardiac arrest (rearrest) after initial return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) is associated with relatively poor outcomes. Early identification of rearrest might allow for intervention to prevent rearrest. In this study, we sought to determine whether clinical ECG features can predict rearrest.

Methods: We performed a retrospective cohort study of adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) patients who achieved ROSC between 2018-2024. We evaluated the association of ECG features (QRS width, standard deviation of NN intervals, root mean square of successive NN interval differences, and percentage of NN intervals that differ by more than 50 milliseconds) within individual 15-second segments throughout a 5-minute window prior to rearrest as well as their temporal trends over the 5-minute analytic window.

Results: Of the 1,489 OHCA patients achieving ROSC, 1,298 were analyzed; 528 (40.7%) experienced rearrest. Rearrest patients were older, less likely to receive bystander CPR (48.7% vs. 61.9%), and had lower survival (20.4% vs. 43.1%) and favorable neurologic outcomes (7.8% vs. 21.2%; all p<0.001). We found lower heart rate, wider QRS, and higher HR variability in those with rearrest. Identification was highest 1 minute prior to rearrest (AUROC 0.74), declining beyond 3 minutes. Models using temporal trends achieved AUROC 0.67; strongest predictors were heart rate variability measures and QRS width.

Conclusion: Established ECG features achieved good prediction for rearrest with identification improving closer to time of rearrest. Future work leveraging novel features or more advanced artificial intelligence models may further improve prediction.

item.title: Lancet: Performance of 0/1 h versus 0/3 h pathways in patients with suspected myocardial infarction: a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
item.description:
Background: In patients with suspected myocardial infarction, the 0/1 h pathway (blood draws at 0 h and 1 h) is recommended in current guidelines for early risk stratification. However, individual trials used different safety outcomes, and efficacy outcomes were inconclusive or not assessed. We conducted a systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis of all randomised controlled trials to synthesise the totality of the evidence, assess heterogeneity across trials, and evaluate clinically relevant outcomes using harmonised definitions across trials.

Methods: In this systematic review and individual participant data meta-analysis, we searched PubMed, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Scopus, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform from inception to July 6, 2026, without language restrictions, for randomised trials comparing the safety and efficacy of 0/1 h versus 0/3 h pathways (blood draws at 0 h and 3 h, ie, standard care). Individual participant data were obtained and outcome definitions were harmonised. The primary analysis used a two-stage random-effects meta-analysis. After receipt of the individual participant data but before data harmonisation or analysis, the primary safety outcome was refined to a composite of all-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction within 30 days, from the originally specified composite of all-cause death or any new myocardial infarction. The primary efficacy outcomes were emergency department length of stay and direct discharge from the emergency department. This meta-analysis is registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261383452).

Findings: Our systematic review identified five randomised trials, all of which provided individual participant data. Among these, the definition of the primary safety outcome varied, and in four trials emergency department length of stay was not reported for the whole analysis population. We included 110 933 patient presentations (55 489 managed with the 0/1 h pathway and 55 444 managed with the 0/3 h pathway). Within 30 days, all-cause death or new type 1 myocardial infarction occurred in 446 patient presentations (0·8%) with the 0/1 h pathway versus 562 patient presentations (1·0%) with the 0/3 h pathway (random-effects pooled odds ratio [OR] 0·83 [95% CI 0·45-1·53]; I2=62·9%; τ2=0·143). Emergency department length of stay was 314 min (IQR 211-481) in the 0/1 h pathway group versus 308 min (209-453) in the 0/3 h pathway group (random-effects pooled geometric mean ratio 1·03 [95% CI 0·85-1·25]; I2=99·2%; τ2=0·024). Direct discharge from the emergency department occurred in 37 190 patient presentations (67·0%) with the 0/1 h pathway versus 36 485 patient presentations (65·8%) with the 0/3 h pathway (random-effects pooled OR 1·31 [95% CI 0·79-2·16]; I2=97·8%; τ2=0·156).

Interpretation: Across the available randomised trials, short-term adverse event rates were low with both pathways, but the pooled safety estimate remained imprecise. On average, earlier cardiac troponin retesting did not reduce emergency department length of stay or clearly increase direct discharge, and substantial between-study heterogeneity indicates that treatment effects might not translate uniformly across health-care systems. For hospitals considering transitioning from a 0/3 h to a 0/1 h pathway, implementation decisions should take broader diagnostic and organisational considerations into account.

item.title: Lancet: Irritable bowel syndrome and related disorders of gut-brain interaction
item.description:
Irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea are disorders of gut-brain interaction, the symptoms of which include abnormal stool consistency or frequency accompanied by varying degrees of abdominal pain, discomfort, bloating, or distension. These conditions affect 20% of the global population with a relapsing and remitting course. Risk factors include female sex, younger age, a history of common mental disorders, and acute enteric infection. The pathophysiology of irritable bowel syndrome, chronic constipation, and functional diarrhoea remain incompletely understood, but are thought to be secondary to aberrant interactions throughout the gut-brain axis, resulting in disordered gut motility and visceral hypersensitivity. These conditions are diagnosed with a combination of clinical history, absence of alarm symptoms-such as weight loss or rectal bleeding-and targeted investigations. An empathetic management approach improves quality of life and symptoms, reduces health-care use, and enhances treatment adherence. Mainstays of treatment include education, dietary and lifestyle advice, modifying fibre intake, and drugs directed towards predominant symptoms. For severe symptoms, other treatments include specific medical devices, biofeedback, or psychological therapies. However, the effectiveness of most treatments is modest and there is an ongoing need to expand available treatments for bowel disorders, with several novel drugs currently in development.

The manosphere, a diffuse commercial ecosystem and loose collection of online communities united by shared beliefs about masculinity, misogyny, and male victimisation, is an under-recognised determinant of health harms. item.title: Lancet: Charting a course to men's health and wellbeing: applying a lens of power and politics to improve men's health outcomes
item.description:
Despite long-standing evidence of poor health and life expectancy outcomes among men, particularly among men who are socially or structurally marginalised, men's health has generally received little and uneven attention in health policy and practice. Its gendered and intersectional aspects have been especially overlooked. This third paper in the Lancet Men's Health Series examines why men's health has received so little policy attention and proposes strategies to raise men's health on national and global agendas. We applied a gender lens to the 3-i theory-based framework and analysed how ideas, interests, and institutions shape the prioritisation of men's health within national and global policy agendas. We review the modest development of men's health policies and assess how power and politics, including the roles of a range of stakeholders from global and national health spaces, commercial actors, and civil society organisations, have shaped the construction of the problem as well as policy attention and framing, resource allocation, and interventions. The scarcity of attention paid to men's health on global and national agendas reflects how power operates through ideas and institutions which contribute to the conflation of gender with women, institutional inertia, and contested constructions of individual versus structural drivers of ill health. We highlight how this has created a space in which commercial actors, including the manosphere, can shape narratives and influence men's health in ways that align with commercial or ideological interests. We conclude by proposing politically informed strategies that recognise how power, institutional arrangements, and competing interests shape men's health policy within prevailing gender and structural orders. We identify entry points for advancing men's health equity and wellbeing that draw on empirical evidence and technical guidance, are grounded in political realities, and are consistent with a commitment to gender justice for all people.

item.title: Lancet: A global men's health epidemiology within an intersectional framework
item.description:
Males have lower life expectancies and greater disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) than females, and particularly poor outcomes are seen among males in marginalised contexts. In this paper, we provide an epidemiological overview and highlight the intersectional nature of men's health. We analyse mortality and DALYs data from the 1990-2023 Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Studies to illustrate our intersectional framework and draw attention to how health varies in men and to show key themes. Conditions that contribute most to the poor health of males include non-communicable diseases (eg, cardiovascular diseases and cancers), substance use, suicide, injuries (eg, road traffic incidents and interpersonal violence), and respiratory infections (eg, tuberculosis and COVID-19). Although cardiovascular disease and cancer make the largest contributions to men's higher mortality rates, determinants of health such as violence and war, migration, economic stagnation, and labour market changes due to automation and new technologies will disproportionally affect their health in the future. Injuries, violence, and other external morbidity causes often occur at a young age and in unequal distributions across the sexes, making a large contribution to DALYs. Although biology plays a role, the pattern of many diseases contributing to health differences reflects the intersection of health behaviours, shaped by patriarchy, ideas of masculinity, and structural drivers (including commercial determinants of health); many of these are preventable. Although improvements in some health behaviours are seen, exceptions occur in marginalising social conditions (eg, incarcerated men, men experiencing homelessness, men with mental illnesses, men with substance use disorders, men with low income, men who have sex with men, and those who are gender non-conforming). Multiple data sources detail men's shorter life expectancies and the drivers compared with women, but going beyond sex disaggregation remains challenging and is an urgent priority for research and health monitoring.

item.title: Lancet: Men's health: an intersectional and multilevel framework for understanding syndemic patterns of health
item.description:
Men occupy a privileged position within gender power relations: the male body has been the default reference point for biomedical research and therapeutic development (with the historical exclusion of women from medical trials), and men dominate health services leadership and exercise well documented medical misogyny. Yet despite their privileged position, many aspects of men's health outcomes are neglected and undertheorised because they are not examined through an intersectional gender lens. Although consideration of gender and masculinity is important for understanding men's health, research thus far has focused predominantly on men's harmful health behaviours, overemphasising individual determinants of health, and a deficit-based approach. Little attention has been paid to the influence of structural determinants of men's health risks and vulnerabilities, or the gender-specific health outcomes of worsening social and economic inequalities. In this first paper of a Lancet Series on men's health, we present a conceptual framework for understanding men's health from an intersectional perspective, highlighting how structural, social, and commercial determinants of health, intersectionality, and syndemic theory can be combined to analyse men's health at different socioecological levels. We illustrate the framework using four selected case studies that show how the health outcomes of marginalised men are influenced by complex interactions. We provide a working definition of men's health that reflects existing literature and builds on the conceptual framework and case studies. Promotion of gender justice and health equity requires moving beyond one-dimensional approaches that construct men as problematic individuals, and towards better understanding and action on the broader set of power systems and structural determinants underpinning men's health.

item.title: Lancet: Non-invasive tests in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease: the LITMUS prospective multicentre diagnostic accuracy study
item.description:
Background: The advent of regulatory-approved pharmacological treatments for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) calls for precise, non-invasive biomarkers that facilitate early diagnosis, support therapy selection, and aid clinical trial enrolment. The European multicentre LITMUS study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of a broad range of non-invasive biomarkers for identifying patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), at-risk MASH, advanced fibrosis, and cirrhosis.

Methods: In this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic accuracy study, adults with biopsy-confirmed MASLD were prospectively recruited across 13 countries in Europe and the USA. We assessed 12 single markers and 18 multimarker panels. The reference standard was centrally scored liver histology according to the non-alcoholic steatohepatitis Clinical Research Network Scoring System. Target conditions included MASH (Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease Activity Score ≥4 with ≥1 point per component), at-risk MASH (MASH plus significant fibrosis [fibrosis stage F≥2]), advanced fibrosis (F≥3), and cirrhosis (F4). Performance was evaluated by area-under-the-receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with the minimum acceptable criterion (MAC) of AUC higher than 0·80 to indicate potential biopsy replacement.

Findings: Between Jan 1, 2018, and June 30, 2023, we analysed data from 1590 participants with centrally scored liver biopsies and at least one biomarker measurement; 609 (38%) had biopsy-confirmed at-risk MASH, 678 (43%) had MASH, 585 (37%) had advanced fibrosis, and 164 (10%) had cirrhosis. For detecting at-risk MASH, SomaSignal showed the highest diagnostic performance (AUC 0·83 [95% CI 0·80-0·85]), significantly exceeding MAC, whereas no other test reached the MAC for MASH only. For advanced fibrosis, SomaSignal showed the highest performance (AUC 0·92 [0·90-0·94]), followed by FibroMeter-VCTE (AUC 0·87 [0·83-0·92]), Agile 3+ and TSP2 (both AUC 0·84 [0·82-0·86]), and NIS4 (0·82 [0·80-0·85]). For cirrhosis, FibroMeter-VCTE showed the highest diagnostic performance (AUC 0·94 [0·90-0·97]) followed by SomaSignal (AUC 0·92 [0·90-0·94]), followed by Agile 3+ (0·88 [0·85-0·91]), Agile 4 (0·87 [0·84-0·90]), ADAPT (0·85 [0·81-0·88]), and ELF, LSM-VCTE, and TSP2 (all 0·84 [0·81-0·87]). Sequential two-step approaches using gamma-glutamyl transferase as a first-line test met the MAC for both advanced fibrosis and at-risk MASH.

Interpretation: Although single markers resulted in variable and limited performance when compared to histology for detecting at-risk MASH, multimarker panels showed great potential, with a proteomic panel showing strong diagnostic performance. These findings could support the selection and implementation of non-invasive testing strategies in MASLD and inform future clinical guidelines, regulatory evaluation, and clinical trial design.

item.title: Lancet: Prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation in early paediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PROSpect): an international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomised controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Data on prone positioning and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) used separately or in combination in patients with paediatric acute respiratory distress syndrome (PARDS) are inconclusive, leading to wide practice variability. We aimed to compare the effects of prone positioning with supine positioning and the effects of HFOV with conventional mechanical ventilation on ventilator-free days in children with early, moderate-to-severe PARDS.

Methods: PROSpect was an international, two-by-two factorial, response-adaptive, phase 3, randomised controlled trial done in 75 paediatric intensive care units in 18 countries. Eligible patients were aged 2 weeks to 20 years, and were intubated and mechanically ventilated for less than 96 h before meeting criteria for moderate-to-severe PARDS. Patients were centrally randomly assigned using a web-based system to supine positioning and conventional mechanical ventilation, prone positioning and conventional mechanical ventilation, supine positioning and HFOV, or prone positioning and HFOV. Initially, the allocation was 1:1:1:1 stratified by age group and direct or indirect lung injury using a permuted block design with blocks of four and eight. Response-adaptive randomisation updates were planned to adjust allocation probabilities 28 days after 300 patients were randomly assigned and then 28 days after every 100 additional patients. Given the nature of the interventions, masking was not possible. The primary outcome was ventilator-free days through to day 28 among all randomly assigned participants. Safety was assessed prospectively by daily monitoring for the occurrence of prespecified adverse events. This study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03896763) and is closed to enrolment.

Findings: Between May 1, 2019 and Jan 13, 2026, 1045 patients were eligible for enrolment. The trial was stopped early for futility and slow enrolment after 424 of 600 planned patients were recruited. 126 patients were randomly assigned to the supine and conventional mechanical ventilation group, 130 to the prone and conventional mechanical ventilation group, 90 to the supine and HFOV group, and 78 to the prone and HFOV group. Median age was 3·3 years (IQR 1·1-10·1), 211 (50%) patients were female, and 213 (50%) were male. There were no significant differences in ventilator-free days between prone and supine positioning (median 17·9 days [IQR 8·9-21·3] vs 17·4 days [6·4-21·9]; Hodges-Lehmann location shift adjusting for ventilation 0·0 [95% CI -0·8 to 1·0]) or between HFOV and conventional mechanical ventilation (17·3 [5·7-21·6] vs 18·0 [9·9-21·5]; Hodges-Lehmann location shift adjusting for positioning -0·3 [95% CI -1·5 to 0·5]). 41 (10%) patients had died at day 28, without group differences. Plugging or obstruction of the artificial airway occurred more frequently with prone than supine positioning (14 events in 12 [6%] of 188 patients vs three events in three [2%] of 197 patients; 0·74 [95% CI 0·44-1·26] vs 0·15 [0·05-0·47] events per 100 artificial airway days; rate ratio 4·83 [95% CI 1·38-16·82]). Stage 2 or worse immobility-related pressure injuries also occurred more frequently with prone versus supine positioning (12 [6%] vs two [1%]; relative risk 6·13 [95% CI 1·45-25·97]). Haemodynamic instability occurred more frequently with HFOV than conventional mechanical ventilation (41 events in 19 [13%] of 141 patients vs 38 events in 22 [9%] of 244 patients; 2·21 [95% CI 1·63-3·00] vs 1·22 [0·89-1·68] events per 100 paediatric intensive care unit days; rate ratio 1·84 [95% CI 1·18-2·87]). One serious adverse event, an unwitnessed self-extubation followed by cardiopulmonary arrest, occurred in a patient in the prone and conventional mechanical ventilation group.

Interpretation: We found no evidence to support prone positioning or HFOV as first-line strategies to improve ventilator-free days in patients with early, moderate-to-severe PARDS. Thus, the routine use of these strategies in this population is not recommended.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Statewide availability of pharmacies in Georgia prepared to dispense buprenorphine or naloxone: A secret shopper study
item.description:
Purpose: To examine access to pharmacies dispensing buprenorphine and naloxone across Georgia.

Procedures: A "secret shopper" method was employed to call all pharmacies in Georgia to determine if buprenorphine and naloxone were available to be dispensed. Logistic regressions examined associations between pharmacy characteristics and stocking medications. Distance to the nearest stocked pharmacy and county-level opioid overdose rates were used to visualize observed trends.

Main findings: Of 2039 pharmacies called, 78% provided complete data. More pharmacies stocked naloxone (64.7%) versus buprenorphine (30.0%). Regional pharmacies had lower odds ratios (OR) of carrying buprenorphine (OR=0.57, 95% CI: 0.42-0.78, p < 0.001) and naloxone (OR=0.64, 95% CI: 0.48-0.85, p = 0.002) compared to national chains. Independent pharmacies demonstrated the same trend for buprenorphine (OR=0.73, 95% CI: 0.56-0.94, P = 0.014) and naloxone (OR= 0.31, 95% CI: 0.24-0.40, p < 0.001) compared to national chains. Rural pharmacies were more likely to carry buprenorphine compared to metropolitan pharmacies (OR=1.89, 95% CI: 1.32-2.69, p < 0.001). At the census tract level, distance to the nearest pharmacy stocked with buprenorphine or naloxone ranged from 0.06 miles to 25.4 miles. Census tracts with a high distance and a high overdose death rate had more residents with lower levels of educational attainment and were less diverse. In metro Atlanta, high distance and high overdose tracts were comprised of more Black residents.

New/important aspects: This is the first statewide analysis of buprenorphine and naloxone availability in Georgia. Similar secret shopper approaches can be adopted to discern availability in other states based on pharmacy and census level characteristics.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Assessing whether self-reported impulsivity, task-based inhibitory control, and early sipping behaviors longitudinally predict adolescent alcohol use and problems in the ABCD study
item.description:
Background: Early low-level alcohol use, impulsivity, and inhibitory control predict subsequent alcohol use and experiencing related problems. However, few studies have examined the unique and incremental contributions of early sipping, impulsivity, and inhibitory control as predictors of adolescent alcohol use over time.

Methods: Data Release 6.0 from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study was used (n = 11,868; 48% Female). Negative binomial generalized linear mixed-effect models examined relationships of sipping at baseline (ages 9-10) and self-reported impulsivity (UPPS-P) and task-based inhibitory control (Flanker task) over time independently and together in one model as predictors of past-year drinks and problematic alcohol use by ages 15-16.

Results: In individual models, lack of perseverance*age predicted past-year drinks. Sipping*age interactions also predicted past-year drinks. In the full model three significant interactions were identified, (1) sipping*age, (2) lack of perseverance*age, and (3) lack of planning*age. Importantly, plots suggest each as a main effect of drinks is not dependent on age. Regarding problematic use, there was a significant interaction in the full model: positive urgency*age (IRR=1.05, p = .04), with plots supporting that this relationship is more pronounced in younger ages in those with low positive urgency. There were no significant results for inhibitory control.

Conclusions: Our results found a positive interaction between positive urgency and age on problematic use, potentially indicating low positive urgency as a vulnerability to experiencing problems associated with alcohol use at younger ages. Understanding facets of impulsivity in the context of adolescent alcohol use is important for prevention and intervention efforts, though caution is warranted given small effect sizes.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: One-year mortality following emergency department visits for stimulant toxicity
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Objective: Rising stimulant-related overdose deaths and emergency department (ED) utilization highlight the need to better characterize outcomes following ED encounters for stimulant toxicity. We sought to determine one-year mortality after ED discharge for stimulant toxicity and to characterize the causes of death.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study used a linked statewide database of ED and hospital discharge records and death records. Patients discharged from the ED with a primary diagnosis of stimulant toxicity, identified by International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes, were included. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality within one year of ED discharge, estimated using Kaplan-Meier analysis. A secondary reference analysis was performed among patients with ED visits for acute opioid toxicity to contextualize mortality estimates against a population previously associated with elevated post-discharge mortality.

Results: A total of 2356 patients met inclusion criteria. One-year mortality was 2.1% (95% confidence interval [CI] 1.6-2.8%). Among patients who died within one year, median age at the index visit was 35 years and median time to death was 118 days (interquartile range [IQR] 63-228 days). Overdose accounted for 67% of deaths, with opioids implicated in 54% and combined opioid-stimulant involvement in 37%. In the secondary reference cohort of 1665 opioid-related ED visits, one-year mortality was 6.9% (95% CI 5.8-8.3%).

Conclusion: Patients with ED encounters for stimulant toxicity experienced substantial one-year mortality in a relatively young population. Subsequent deaths were predominantly overdose-related and frequently opioid-involved, supporting consideration of opioid-focused harm-reduction interventions in this population.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Disparities in investigation of physical abuse among trauma patients
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Physical abuse is a significant public health issue in the United States, leading to poor health outcomes such as chronic illness, depression, and substance abuse. Research regarding how the medical system addresses physical abuse in the overall adult population is scarce. The objective of this study was to assess disparities in investigation of physical abuse among adult trauma patients.

Methods: This is a retrospective analysis of the 2017-2019 American College of Surgeons-Trauma Quality Program database. This study included all adult patients (≥18 years) who had a report of physical abuse by the medical team to authorities. Chi square and multivariate analysis were applied where appropriate to assess which characteristics showed disparities in investigation rate.

Results: On univariate analysis, there were disparities with regard to age, mechanism, race, ethnicity, payment method, and mental health or substance use disorder. On multivariate analysis, male sex, non-penetrating trauma, age ≥70, American Indian race, and presence of a mental health disorder were associated with decreased odds of investigation. Non-elderly adult patients made up a disproportionate amount of abuse victims.

Conclusions: This study shows significant disparities in the escalation of a physical abuse report to an official investigation in the trauma setting. The authors recommend increased advocacy and resource allocation for these vulnerable populations in the clinical setting as well as further research regarding to what extent patient choice versus discretion of authorities influences these disparities. The authors also recommend a larger research focus on non-elderly adult victims of abuse.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Tongue capillary refill time and imaging parameters for acute coronary syndrome identification: A prospective ED study
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Rapid identification of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) in emergency department (ED) patients with chest pain remains challenging. Tongue capillary refill time (CRT) and tongue imaging may reflect systemic perfusion, but their value in ACS is unknown.

Objective: To evaluate the diagnostic performance of standardized tongue-derived perfusion, macroscopic, and imaging parameters for identifying ACS.

Methods: This prospective observational study enrolled 208 consecutive adult ED patients presenting with chest pain. Standardized tongue imaging and tongue CRT were assessed. A separate 20-patient pilot assessed interobserver reliability using ICC and kappa coefficients. Blinded ACS adjudication used clinical findings, serial high-sensitivity troponin measurements, electrocardiography, imaging studies, specialist consultations, and follow-up data. ROC analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed.

Results: Among 208 patients, 61 (29.3%) had ACS: 16 STEMI, 41 NSTEMI, and four unstable angina cases. Tongue CRT was significantly prolonged in ACS patients (2.6 [2.2-2.9] vs. 1.3 [1.1-1.6] seconds; p<0.001). Tongue CRT demonstrated excellent discrimination for ACS (AUC 0.941, 95% CI 0.903-0.980), outperforming the HEART score (0.860), admission troponin (0.831), and TIMI score (0.788). A CRT threshold ≥2s yielded 86.9% sensitivity and 93.2% specificity. Tongue CRT and macroscopically dry tongue remained associated with ACS after adjustment (both p<0.001). Quantitative RGB and HSV parameters showed no significant between-group differences.

Conclusions: Standardized tongue CRT showed excellent discrimination for ACS in this cohort, in which most ACS cases were myocardial infarction. Its diagnostic value in unstable angina and incremental clinical utility remain unestablished. External validation is required before routine clinical use.
