item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Purpose: The objective of this study was to introduce a novel closed reduction technique, termed the FEAT (Fixation, External rotation, Alignment, Traction) method, for anterior shoulder dislocations and to evaluate its effectiveness, speed, reliability, and safety.

Methods: This prospective study enrolled 30 patients presenting with anterior glenohumeral dislocation at the Emergency or Orthopedics outpatient department of Hubei Provincial Hospital. Closed reduction was performed using the FEAT method without administering analgesics, muscle relaxants, or anesthetics. Only a single reduction attempt was permitted per patient. The time required for successful reduction was recorded, and patient-reported pain intensity during the procedure was assessed using a visual analog scale (VAS) ranging from 0 to 10.

Results: All 30 patients experienced successful reduction on the first attempt. The average time required for successful reduction was 54.3 s, with a mean VAS pain score of 3.67 during the procedure.

Conclusion: The FEAT method is an effective, rapid, and minimally painful technique for anterior shoulder dislocation reduction. Its simplicity and ease of mastery support its widespread clinical adoption.

item.description:
Objectives: Documented substance use disorders (SUDs) are common among hospitalized adults and contribute to healthcare utilization. We examined factors associated with documented SUDs and evaluated whether hospital length of stay (LOS) and facility costs varied according to SUD diagnosis position and major SUD subtype.

Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study using the 2021 Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project National Inpatient Sample. Documented SUDs were identified using ICD-10-CM codes F10-F16 and F18-F19 in any diagnosis position; tobacco-related disorders (F17) were evaluated in a sensitivity analysis. Survey-weighted regression models examined factors associated with documented SUDs and compared adjusted LOS and inflation-adjusted facility costs by diagnosis position and major SUD subtype.

Results: Among 6,666,752 sampled discharges representing 33.3 million US hospitalizations, documented SUDs were identified in 10.8% of hospitalizations. Greater comorbidity burden was the strongest independent predictor of documented SUDs (adjusted OR: 1.49; 95% CI: 1.48-1.49). Secondary-diagnosis SUD hospitalizations had longer adjusted LOS than hospitalizations without documented SUDs, whereas principal-diagnosis SUD hospitalizations had shorter LOS. Opioid-related disorders demonstrated the greatest excess LOS and were the only major subtype associated with higher adjusted facility costs.

Conclusions: Hospital utilization varied substantially according to SUD diagnosis position and subtype. Aggregating documented SUDs obscured clinically important differences, particularly among secondary opioid-related disorders. These findings support subtype-specific inpatient addiction medicine strategies.

item.title: J Addict Med: Nonfatal Overdose and Naloxone Possession Among Homeless Adults in California Who Use Illicit Substances
item.description:
Objective: To determine the prevalence and factors associated with nonfatal overdose and naloxone possession among homeless adults who use illicit substances.

Methods: We used representative cross-sectional data from the California Statewide Study of People Experiencing Homelessness (2021-2022; n=3200), restricting our sample to participants reporting illicit substance use. Our outcomes were recent nonfatal overdose and current naloxone possession. We calculated weighted frequency distributions and conducted separate unadjusted and adjusted Poisson regression models to examine the association between 3 exposures (age of first homelessness, shelter status, and length homeless) and the 2 outcomes.

Results: The study population was racially diverse, two-thirds were men, with mean age of 46.1. Half used any illicit substances (49.6%, n=1277), of which 17.8% experienced a nonfatal overdose and 39.2% carried naloxone. In adjusted models, increasing age of first homelessness was associated with lower nonfatal overdose prevalence ratio [PR]=0.88 (95% CI: 0.78-0.99) and naloxone possession (PR=0.92, 95% CI: 0.86-0.99). Those unsheltered outdoors (PR=2.46, 95% CI: 1.56-3.89) and in vehicles (PR=1.66, 95% CI: 0.96-2.86) (reference=sheltered) and those homeless for >1-≤3 years (PR=1.34, 95% CI: 0.74-2.42) and ≥3 years (PR=2.59, 95% CI: 1.79-3.75) (reference= ≤1 year) had a higher prevalence of nonfatal overdose. Those unsheltered outdoors (PR=1.14, 95% CI: 0.96-2.08) and in vehicles (PR=1.62, 95% CI: 1.06-2.49) had a higher prevalence of naloxone possession.

Conclusions: Nonfatal overdose is high (<1% in general US population), while naloxone possession was low. Efforts to expand overdose prevention and naloxone access to people experiencing homelessness, particularly racially minoritized groups, those in rural areas, and those unsheltered outdoors and with longer homelessness episodes, may reduce preventable overdoses.

item.description:
Objectives: Patient advocates and online commentary have characterized immunotherapeutic approaches for opioid use disorder (OUD) as fundamentally misguided. We aimed to evaluate perspectives in the primary stakeholders, people who use opioids nonmedically (PWUOs).

Methods: We randomized respondents to 3 different survey versions, testing how acceptance of opioid vaccines is influenced by calling them "vaccines" (with minimal information or additional information) versus "long-acting medications." This survey experiment was conducted between June 2024 and June 2025 in 442 US-based adults, 18 or older, who reported past 6-month nonmedical use of opioids or past 6-month use of methadone or buprenorphine for OUD. The primary outcome measure was willingness to use a long-acting blockade-based treatment designed to the participant's preferred duration of blockade (eg, 2-3 mo, lifelong) and targeted substances (eg, heroin, fentanyl, methamphetamine, cannabis, nicotine).

Results: There were 442 respondents (52.7% women; mean age 38.9, SD 9.4; mean DSM-5 OUD criteria met 8/11, SD 3.5). Most respondents were willing to use a long-acting blockade. Willingness was higher when the treatment was described as a "medication" versus a "vaccine" with less versus more descriptive vaccine information ("very" or "kind of willing": medication=134/150, 89%; vaccine with less information=108/142, 76%; vaccine with more information=113/150, 75%). Respondents preferred a duration of action <1 year, primarily targeting fentanyl.

Conclusions: PWUOs expressed willingness to use anti-opioid vaccines, but with strong preferences for limits on duration of action and breadth of blockade. Uptake may increase if opioid vaccines offer a range of breadths and durations of action.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Immunological signatures of sepsis in abdominal solid organ transplant recipients: A multilayer and multicentric prospective cohort study
item.description:
Background: Sepsis is defined as life-threatening organ dysfunction resulting from a dysregulated host response to infection. Patients with prior abdominal solid organ transplantation (SOT) are highly susceptible to infection due to chronic immunosuppression, yet exhibit improved survival once sepsis occurs. The underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood.

Methods: We conducted a post hoc analysis within a prospective multicenter cohort of septic patients (SepsisDataNet.NRW; n = 538). Clinical outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. Immune profiling included serum cytokines, flow cytometric immunophenotyping, plasma proteomics, and intracellular signaling using proximity ligation assays (PLA) in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). To reduce clinical confounding, complementary exploratory analyses were performed in a non-septic kidney transplant cohort (e:KID).

Results: SOT patients demonstrated improved 30-day survival compared with non-SOT patients (84% vs. 66%; adjusted HR 0.49, 95% CI 0.26-0.95). Cytokine analysis revealed lower IL-6 and TNF-α levels alongside higher IL-18 concentrations, indicating an altered inflammatory profile. Flow cytometry showed reductions in adaptive immune cells but relatively preserved innate immune function, reflected by higher monocytic HLA-DR expression. Proteomics identified enrichment of innate immune, complement, and lipid metabolic response networks. PLA-based cellular analyses revealed increased GLUT1 expression and enhanced TFAM/TFB2M interaction in SOT patients, indicating a distinct immunometabolic marker profile. In e:KID patients paired serum metabolomics demonstrated higher glucose and lower lactate concentrations 12 months after transplantation, accompanied by broader alterations in lipid and branched-chain amino acid profiles.

Conclusion: In patients with sepsis, abdominal SOT is associated with significant better survival than in non-SOT patients. Septic abdominal SOT patients display a distinct immune phenotype characterized by attenuated systemic inflammation, relative preservation of selected innate immune readouts, and alterations in immunometabolic markers.

item.title: Intensive Care Med: Ventilator-associated pneumonia after traumatic brain injury: a timing-sensitive ecological framework of neuroimmune-pulmonary vulnerability
item.description:
Background: Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) is frequent after traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its biological meaning and outcome impact remain incompletely defined. Traditional models emphasise mechanical ventilation, aspiration, colonisation, endotracheal tube biofilm, and hospital pathogens. These mechanisms remain essential, but they do not fully explain the early clustering, heterogeneous susceptibility, changing bacteriology, and variable mortality effect observed after TBI.

Main text: Severe brain injury creates an early vulnerable host state through impaired consciousness and airway protection, neuroimmune dysregulation, autonomic and endocrine activation, altered pulmonary immune surveillance, and, in many patients, extracranial trauma, shock, transfusion, or thoracic injury. These processes interact with ventilation, antibiotic pressure, and rapid respiratory microbiome disruption. Early VAP may reflect abrupt loss of control after injury and intubation, whereas late VAP may reflect persistent or secondary failure driven by biofilm maturation, antibiotic selection, multidrug-resistant pathogens, and intensive care unit (ICU)-acquired immune dysfunction. Clinically, VAP consistently prolongs ventilation, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and resource use, while its independent effect on mortality is phenotype- and context-dependent.

Conclusions: This model proposes a timing-sensitive ecological framework in which established mechanisms may converge early and with particular clinical intensity after severe TBI, creating a vulnerable host-microbe state that may lower the threshold for clinically apparent infection. Future studies should distinguish isolated TBI from polytrauma, compare TBI with other acute brain injuries and non-neurological ventilated populations, and incorporate dynamic immune, microbial, and trajectory-based outcomes.

Highlights: VAP after TBI should be viewed as a timing-sensitive interaction between ventilator exposure and early host vulnerability, not as a distinct disease entity or as a pneumonia pathway unique to traumatic brain injury. The TBI-focused contribution lies in the early convergence of otherwise non-unique mechanisms: impaired airway control, aspiration risk, neuroimmune-endocrine activation, treatment exposure, dysbiosis, and extracranial injury burden, rather than in any single TBI-specific mechanism. Isolated TBI and TBI with polytrauma are biologically different phenotypes and should be separated in future studies. Early and late VAP may represent different phases of loss of pulmonary host-microbe containment; this distinction is probabilistic rather than TBI-specific in itself and requires validation in TBI-stratified cohorts. Mortality remains clinically relevant but context-dependent; VAP more consistently modifies recovery trajectory, ventilator dependence, ICU stay, antibiotic exposure, and possibly neurological recovery.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Preterm Birth and Birth Weight and Cognitive Performance Among Males Eligible for Military Service
item.description:
Importance: Preterm birth and low birth weight are associated with adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes in childhood, but their association with cognitive performance in young adulthood remains incompletely characterized at the population level.

Objective: To determine whether gestational age and birth weight are associated with cognitive performance during compulsory military service in young adult males.

Design, setting, and participants: This nationwide retrospective register-based cohort study included males born in Finland between January 1, 1987, and December 31, 1998 (N = 350 617), identified using linked national health and military registers. The dataset was based on cognitive testing conducted during military service at a mean age of 19 to 20 years. Preconscription deaths and individuals without military cognitive testing data were excluded. Data analysis was performed from June 1 to December 31, 2025.

Exposures: Gestational age at birth and birth weight.

Main outcomes and measures: Cognitive performance was measured using the Finnish Defense Forces' cognitive basic test 1, consisting of verbal, numerical, and visuospatial subtests. Scores were standardized on a 9-point scale (mean [SD], 5.00 [1.96]), with the overall score calculated as the mean of the 3 subtests.

Results: A total of 192 767 participants were included, of whom 10 016 (5.2%) were born preterm. Individuals born extremely preterm scored lower on the overall cognitive test compared with full-term individuals (mean difference, -0.78 [95% CI, -1.07 to -0.49] points). The groups born very preterm and moderately preterm showed progressively smaller deficits, while those born late preterm showed minimal differences compared with their peers born full term. Associations reached a plateau at approximately 36 to 38 gestational weeks. Similar dose-response associations were observed across birth weight categories, with individuals with extremely low birth weight scoring 0.89 (95% CI, -1.23 to -0.55) points lower than those with normal birth weight. Differences were most pronounced in visuospatial and numerical subtests, whereas verbal performance showed little or no association with gestational age or birth weight.

Conclusions and relevance: Lower gestational age and birth weight were associated with poorer cognitive performance in young adulthood in a dose-response pattern, with the largest differences observed among individuals born extremely preterm and with very low birth weight. Late preterm birth was associated with minimal cognitive differences. These findings underscore the long-term cognitive impact of preterm birth.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Data Extraction Errors and Diagnostic Conclusions of Meta-Analyses: A Systematic Review
item.description:
Importance: Systematic reviews (SRs) are often characterized as being inherently reproducible; however, errors arising from the evidence synthesis process can compromise this assumption and lead to reproducibility failure.

Objective: To investigate the data extraction errors in diagnostic meta-analyses and the extent to which such errors affect the results of meta-analyses.

Evidence review: We included SRs with diagnostic meta-analyses from the Cochrane Library filtered by diagnostic up to May 2023. Data used in the original meta-analyses were extracted from the included SRs and independently reproduced from primary studies. Data extraction errors were identified by comparing datasets and classified by potential mechanism. To assess the consequences, we reanalyzed the meta-analyses using error-corrected data with the same effect estimators and methods. The primary outcomes were the proportions of data extraction errors at the trial, meta-analysis, and SR levels. The secondary outcome was the consequences for diagnostic performance measures (eg, sensitivity, specificity, diagnostic odds ratio [DOR], and area under the curve [AUC]). Analysis was conducted between March and June 2026.

Findings: A total of 46 SRs, 879 diagnostic comparisons, and 6173 primary studies were included. Data extraction could not be reproduced in 338 studies (5.5%) and affected 137 diagnostic meta-analyses (33.1%) and 34 SRs (73.9%). Numerical error (ie, incorrect values) and inferential error (ie, incorrect derivation from statistics) were the most prevalent error types, accounting for 166 of 412 (40.3%) and 140 of 412 (34.0%) errors, respectively. Mismatching error (ie, mismatching data to groups; 69 of 412 errors [16.7%]) and conceptual error (ie, misaligned reference details; 37 of 412 [9.0%]) were also identified. Among 137 reproduced meta-analyses, large changes were observed in 0.7% meta-analyses for sensitivity (absolute differences, >0.20), 3.6% for DOR (fold-changes, >5.0), and 2.9% for AUC (absolute differences, >0.10). Regression analysis of error location showed that combined false-positive and true-negative errors were associated with higher likelihood of moderate or large DOR changes (OR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.01-1.22).

Conclusions and relevance: In this SR of diagnostic meta-analyses in Cochrane reviews, data extraction errors were common and differentially affected performance measures, highlighting the need to implement rigorous data extraction processes and to consider careful selection of performance measures.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Ambient Temperature and Heart Failure Hospitalizations in Older Adults in the US
item.description:
Importance: The U-shaped association between ambient temperature and cardiovascular mortality is well established. However, limited knowledge exists about the association between ambient temperature and heart failure (HF) hospitalizations, particularly among older adults in the US. Understanding this association is essential to informing climate adaptation strategies and health policies.

Objective: To assess the association between daily ambient temperature exposure and HF hospitalization among Medicare beneficiaries both nationally and by climate region.

Design, setting, and participants: This time-stratified case-crossover study included older adults (aged ≥65 years) hospitalized for HF between January 1, 2007, and December 31, 2022, based on Medicare claims data. Cases were defined as emergency department visits leading to HF hospitalization with up to 4 controls, or nonevent days, matched for the same patient on day of week, month, and year. The data analysis was performed between June 2025 and August 2026.

Exposure: Daily mean ambient temperature derived from the Parameter-Elevation Relationships on Independent Slopes Model linked through residential zip code.

Main outcomes and measures: The association between mean temperature exposure and HF hospitalization was estimated nationally and by 9 climate regions (Central, East North Central, Northeast, Northwest, South, Southeast, Southwest, West, West North Central) using conditional logit for distributed lag nonlinear models (reference, 75 °F). A 14-day lag was used for mean temperatures less than 75 °F and 0-day lag for mean temperatures greater than 75 °F.

Results: A total of 1 517 756 HF hospitalizations from 996 312 patients (mean [SD] age, 78.0 [8.2] years, 60.3% female) were identified. Colder ambient temperatures were associated with increased HF hospitalizations nationally. At the regional fifth percentile temperature compared with 75 °F, the largest associations were observed in the West North Central (n = 17 286 [1.1%]; odds ratio [OR], 1.62; 95% CI, 1.25-2.11), West (n = 107 911 [7.1%]; OR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.28-1.53), Southwest (n = 30 536 [2.0%]; OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.11-1.62), and Northwest (n = 33 353 [2.2%]; OR, 1.34; 95% CI, 1.08-1.65) regions. Temperatures greater than 75 °F were not associated with increased HF hospitalization.

Conclusions and relevance: This study found that among Medicare beneficiaries, colder ambient temperatures were associated with increased HF hospitalizations, whereas warmer temperatures were not. The U-shaped temperature-cardiovascular risk association described for cardiovascular mortality and other cardiovascular outcomes did not apply for HF hospitalizations among older adults in the US. These findings suggest that ongoing region-specific surveillance of heat- and cold-related HF hospitalization risk will be essential, particularly in areas with limited adaptive capacity.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Financial Functioning Before Mental Health Disclosure to a Retail Bank
item.description:
Importance: Financial functioning is an important dimension of mental health, affecting independence and overall functioning. However, there is uncertainty about how financial functioning evolves over time and across mental health conditions, with current evidence largely relying on survey or experimental data.

Objective: To evaluate whether financial functioning differs in the period preceding mental health disclosure to a bank and whether differences are shared or condition specific.

Design, setting, and participants: In this case-control study, deidentified banking records from a major UK bank were used to compare financial indicators between individuals with a bank-disclosed mental health condition between January 2019 and August 2025 and controls, matched 1:3. Analyses were conducted between July 2025 and March 2026.

Exposures: Bank-recorded mental health disclosures mapped to diagnostic groupings of mental, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental conditions.

Main outcomes and measures: A total of 331 monthly financial indicators were used to capture financial functioning. A 2-stage bayesian hierarchical model examined how variation in case-control differences was distributed across financial indicators, conditions, and their interaction.

Results: The case group comprised 18 428 individuals with mental health disclosures (mean [SD] age, 41.5 [13.9] years; 10 357 women [56%]) and the control group included 64 229 individuals (mean [SD] age, 40.9 [14.5] years; 36 052 women [56%]). Differences in financial functioning were evident up to 36 months before disclosure. Compared with controls, posterior mean estimates for cases showed higher welfare-related income (disability benefits: 0.80; 95% credible interval [CrI], 0.78-0.83), greater financial distress (credit scores: -0.52 [95% CrI, -0.55 to -0.49]; overdraft use: 0.49 [95% CrI, 0.47-0.52]), and more frequent bank interaction (eg, telephone banking use: 0.56 [95% CrI, 0.53-0.58]). Additional differences included higher cash use and reduced spending on self-care and recreational activities among cases (standardized differences ≤0.4 SD units). Variance decomposition indicated that most variation was attributable to differences across financial indicators (SD, 0.11; 88% of total variance), with negligible variation explained by condition (SD, 0.01; <1%) and a small contribution from interaction effects (SD, 0.04; 12%), indicating broadly consistent patterns across conditions.

Conclusions and relevance: In this case-control study of bank customers, those who disclosed a mental health condition differed from controls across a range of financial indicators preceding the disclosure, with similar patterns across conditions. The findings suggest that banking data may provide objective measures of financial functioning to inform support strategies in banking and clinical contexts.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: User Interface Designs to Address Cancer Misinformation: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Misinformation about false and potentially harmful cancer treatments is common on social media. Strategies are needed to encourage reporting to reduce exposure to inaccurate treatment claims.

Objective: To evaluate the impact of 2 user interface designs (prompts on posts) on intervening and sharing cancer misinformation on social media.

Design, setting, and participants: This 3-group, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial assessed outcomes at 5 time points from March 31 to May 12, 2025. US adults (ages 18-65 years) who had a cancer diagnosis or identified as a cancer caregiver and used social media were recruited from Prolific. Participants interacted with cancer misinformation posts on a simulated realistic social media platform. Data were analyzed from May 13, 2025, to July 27, 2026.

Interventions: Participants were randomized to cancer misinformation posts shown with social cue-enhanced prompts that specify others' actions and a review policy, standard prompts, or no prompts (control).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was a participant flagging a post to intervene. Primary and secondary outcomes included recorded social media behavior (flagging, disliking, liking) and self-reported willingness to flag, dislike, like, comment, and share about the posts. Intervening outside the study platform was also assessed. A separate generalized estimating equations model was used for each outcome.

Results: A total of 294 individuals (mean [SD] age, 39.3 [11.7] years; 179 [62%] women) with cancer or who were caregivers for individuals with cancer were randomized, with 88 participants receiving social cue prompts, 92 receiving standard prompts, and 114 receiving no prompts. Posts with inaccurate claims were flagged 2 to 3 times more often with social cue (224 of 592 posts [38%]) and standard (180 of 689 posts [26%]) prompts than those without prompts (84 of 675 posts [12%]) (social cue vs control: rate ratio [RR], 3.12 [95% CI, 1.79-5.42]; standard vs control: RR, 2.15 [95% CI, 1.20-3.88]). Prompts led to less sharing behavior (ie, liking: 20 posts [3%] with social cue prompts; 10 posts [1%] with standard prompts) compared with posts without prompts (65 posts [10%]) (social cue vs control: RR, 0.07 [95% CI, 0.04-0.15]; standard vs control: RR, 0.13 [95% CI, 0.04-0.42]). Prompts also led to greater willingness to flag and dislike (intervening) and less willingness to like and share compared with no prompt. Standard prompts led to more flagging on existing social media (outside the study platform) than no prompts.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of user interface designs, simple prompts encouraged responsible behavior online. Prompts on posts led to more intervening and less sharing of cancer misinformation.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Studies of US Department of Health and Human Services Agency Advisory Committees: A Systematic Review
item.description:
Importance: Federal advisory committees provide external expertise and public input to inform regulatory and policy decision-making across agencies within the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). Concerns persist about their use, composition, conflicts of interest (COIs), deliberation, transparency, and influence on agency decisions.

Objective: To identify and characterize original research studies evaluating the implementation and impact of advisory committees convened by HHS agencies since enactment of the Federal Advisory Committee Act.

Evidence review: MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, HeinOnline, EconLit, SSRN, the National Bureau of Economic Research, the HHS Office of Inspector General, the Government Accountability Office, and Google were searched for English-language original studies published from October 6, 1972, through April 10, 2025. Eligible studies characterized the implementation and impact of advisory committees advising agencies within HHS. Studies were categorized by agency and topic domains: meeting use and management, composition, deliberation content and voting, and regulatory impact and performance. Findings within each topic domain were extracted.

Findings: Among 146 included studies published between 1974 and 2025, 91 (62.3%) were peer-reviewed research articles and 55 (37.7%) were non-peer-reviewed studies. Most studies examined advisory committees convened by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA; 132 studies [90.4%]), with fewer studies focusing on those convened by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (5 studies [3.4%]), National Institutes of Health (5 studies [3.4%]), and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (2 studies [1.4%]). Meeting use and management was the most commonly examined topic domain (98 studies [67.1%]). Five of the 13 secondary topic domains (38.5%) included only FDA studies, and no secondary topic domain included more than 2 studies (1.4%) on any single non-FDA HHS agency. Key findings included continued use of FDA advisory committees over time despite wide variation across product types and a decline after 2010, a recent increase in FDA advisory committee members' COIs after a substantial decline following the FDA Amendments Act, and generally high concordance between advisory committee recommendations and agency decisions.

Conclusions and relevance: In this systematic review of original research studies, evidence on HHS advisory committees was concentrated largely on those convened by FDA. Variation in advisory committee use and management, ongoing COI concerns, and limited evidence on advisory committees convened by HHS agencies other than FDA suggest opportunities for reform and the need for more studies evaluating advisory committee implementation and impact across HHS.

item.description:
We cannot know how artificial intelligence (AI) will ultimately change critical care, only that it is driving substantial change quickly. Through ten parables, we describe plausible benefits, harms, and trade-offs involving prognosis, monitoring, liability, research, clinical work, data governance, education, and triage. These parables are not predictions. They are intended to help clinicians, institutions, and regulators envision a range of potential scenarios and think broadly about which applications to pursue, which risks to consider, and which rules to establish before AI systems become entrenched. Each parable reveals how the outlook for AI in critical care is characterized by uncertainty. This includes uncertainty about what a single prediction means for the patient in front of us, how an application built and tested in one setting performs in another, accountability frameworks, professional practice and learning, patient privacy and autonomy, and more. Within each parable we try to keep visible what current evidence already supports and what remains speculative. We close with a set of questions designed to focus that speculation among the interested parties who will shape the future of AI in critical care.

item.description:
Objectives: To develop and internally validate a multivariable prediction model for survival to hospital discharge after pediatric extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation (ECPR) for in-hospital cardiac arrest (IHCA), and to use this model to derive risk-standardized survival rates (RSSRs) and quantify between-hospital variation in outcomes.

Design: Retrospective multicenter cohort study.

Setting: Hospitals contributing to the Extracorporeal Life Support Organization (ELSO) registry between 2020 and 2023.

Patients: Children (< 18 yr) treated with ECPR for IHCA.

Interventions: None.

Measurements and main results: Eligible patients were identified from the ELSO Registry and split into derivation (N = 1060) and validation (N = 317) cohorts using a hospital-stratified split to preserve within-hospital clustering. Survival prediction models were derived using penalized logistic regression with the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator. A full-event model incorporating 14 routinely available clinical variables demonstrated fair discrimination (area under the curve, 0.728 in the derivation cohort and 0.678 in the validation cohort) and good calibration (observed-to-expected ratio, 0.995; Brier score, 0.222 in the validation cohort). This model was embedded in a multilevel logistic regression model to generate hospital-level RSSRs for centers reporting five or more ECPR cases. Between-hospital variation was quantified using the median odds ratio, which was 1.30 (95% CI, 1.11-1.93), indicating significant differences in survival likelihood between centers after adjusting for patient-level risk.

Conclusions: In a large, international cohort of pediatric ECPR patients, we developed and internally validated a clinically interpretable model for survival to hospital discharge. The model performance as a discriminator likely limits its use as a standalone tool for clinical decision-making. However, strong internal calibration allowed for determination of hospital-level RSSRs, which revealed significant inter-hospital variability. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of developing a risk-adjustment model capable of estimating hospital-level RSSRs. Additional external validation and evaluation of residual case-mix differences are needed before such models can be used for benchmarking across pediatric ECPR centers.

Background: Subspecialty interstitial lung disease (ILD) clinics are associated with improved outcomes, yet access remains uneven. Even within tertiary health systems, patients with ILD are managed across diverse ambulatory settings, with unclear implications for care and outcomes.

Research question: Within a single academic health system, do patient characteristics, care delivery, and outcomes differ between individuals with ILD managed in a subspecialty ILD clinic versus other ambulatory settings?

Study design and methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults with ILD at a large academic medical center. Identified patients were stratified by care in a subspecialty ILD clinic versus non-specialty setting. Demographic, diagnostic testing, treatment, health care utilization, and survival data were extracted from the electronic health record. Diagnostic and treatment measures were analyzed using multivariable logistic regression. Hospitalization, emergency department visit, and death were analyzed as time-to-event outcomes.

Results: Among 6,637 patients with ILD, 4,371 (66%) were seen in the subspecialty ILD clinic. The 2,266 patients (34%) managed in non-specialty settings were more likely to identify as Black or Latinx, reside in more socioeconomically deprived neighborhoods, and have an unspecified ILD diagnosis (all p < 0.001). In the peri-diagnostic period, ILD clinic care was associated with higher adjusted odds of chest CT imaging (OR 2.51, 2.07-3.05) and antifibrotic therapy (OR 1.54, 1.32-1.80), and lower odds of lung biopsy (OR 0.47, 0.32-0.68). ILD clinic care was associated with a lower adjusted hazards of all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.46, 0.42-0.51), emergency department visit (HR 0.68, 0.59-0.78), and death (HR 0.57, 0.45-0.72). P-value <0.001 for all.

Interpretation: Within a single health system, subspecialty ILD clinic care was associated with more guideline-concordant care and improved outcomes. Differences in access to subspecialty expertise may contribute to inequities in care delivery, underscoring the need for scalable strategies, referral optimization, telemedicine, and clinical decision support, to extend ILD expertise and improve outcomes.

item.title: Chest: Azithromycin Exposure and Incident Nontuberculous Mycobacterial Isolation in Bronchiectasis and COPD: A Nationwide Nested Case-Control Study
item.description:
Background: Azithromycin reduces exacerbations in chronic airway disease, but whether it alters the risk of nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) isolation is unresolved.

Research question: Is azithromycin exposure in the preceding year associated with incident respiratory NTM isolation in non-cystic fibrosis bronchiectasis and in COPD?

Study design and methods: Two nationwide register-based nested case-control analyses in Denmark. Case patients had a first positive respiratory culture for NTM; controls, alive and free of prior NTM isolation on the index date, were matched 1:20 on age, sex, and comorbidity index. The prespecified exposure was at least 3,000 mg of azithromycin with at least two prescriptions redeemed in the preceding 12 months, with a 3-month lag. Conditional logistic regression was adjusted for inhaled and oral corticosteroids. Exploratory analyses examined an active comparator at matched thresholds, recency, and outcome stringency.

Results: The analyses comprised 173 cases and 3,409 controls (bronchiectasis) and 365 and 7,300 (COPD). Under the prespecified definition, azithromycin was not associated with incident NTM isolation (bronchiectasis: OR, 1.31; 95% CI, 0.79-2.18; COPD: 1.29; 0.78-2.13). In COPD, the OR was 1.61 (1.14-2.28) for one or more prescriptions and 1.29 (0.78-2.13) for two or more. The COPD association was concentrated within 90 days of the index date (2.55; 1.73-3.76) and attenuated with microbiological stringency (definite isolates: 0.77; 0.27-2.20). Non-macrolide antibacterials were more strongly associated than azithromycin at every matched threshold in bronchiectasis (one or more prescriptions: 1.90 [1.36-2.65] vs 1.15 [0.75-1.75]), and at the two higher thresholds in COPD (two or more: 1.48 [1.17-1.86] vs 1.24 [0.75-2.05]).

Interpretation: Azithromycin was not associated with NTM isolation under the prespecified definition. Associations under broader definitions were not dose-dependent and clustered close to the index date, more consistent with indication-driven testing than a drug effect, although in COPD an association with any exposure persisted after accounting for other antibacterials.

item.title: Resuscitation: Traumatic Emergency Thoracotomy for Resuscitation in Shock (TETRiS): a national service evaluation of resuscitative thoracotomy practice outside the operating theatre
item.description:
Background: Resuscitative thoracotomy (RT) is performed in patients with traumatic cardiac arrest or peri-arrest to treat potentially reversible causes of circulatory collapse. Optimal patient selection and timing remain uncertain, and existing evidence is largely retrospective, often excluding prehospital deaths. This prospective service evaluation examined contemporary RT practice and outcomes across a national major trauma system, including prehospital and emergency department settings.

Methods: Prospective 12-month observational study across 20 UK Helicopter Emergency Medical Services and 26 Major Trauma Centre Emergency Departments, using the PHOTON, TERN, and NaTRIC research networks.

Results: A total of 116 patients underwent RT, of which 82 (70.7%) were performed prehospital. Median age was 30 years, 97 patients (83.6%) were male, and 81 (69.8%) sustained penetrating injury. Suspected cardiac tamponade was the most common indication for RT (72/116 [62.1%]), although operative findings demonstrated exsanguinating haemorrhage in 82 patients (70.7%). Overall, 50 patients (43.1%) achieved return of spontaneous circulation and eight (6.9%) survived to hospital discharge. Survival was strongly associated with pathophysiological cause, duration of arrest, and physiological state at the time of intervention, with substantially better outcomes observed in patients with cardiac tamponade than exsanguination. Patients undergoing emergency department RT demonstrated shorter arrest durations, more favourable physiology, and higher survival than those undergoing prehospital RT. There were no survivors beyond 10 minutes of traumatic cardiac arrest.

Conclusion: In this prospective national evaluation of RT practice, outcomes were strongly associated with the pathophysiological cause and duration of arrest, and the residual physiology present at the time of intervention. The most favourable outcomes were observed in patients with cardiac tamponade and those undergoing RT before irreversible physiological deterioration.

item.title: Am J Emerg Med: Latent class phenotypes and emergency department disposition for patients with traumatic subdural hematoma and midline shift
item.category: The American journal of emergency medicine
item.description:
Background: Guidelines recommend surgical evacuation for traumatic subdural hematoma (SDH) with >5 mm midline shift (MLS), but emergency department (ED) triage varies between the operating room (OR) and the intensive care unit (ICU). We investigated whether ED disposition to the OR versus ICU was associated with differences in outcomes and whether distinct patient phenotypes modified these associations.

Methods: We retrospectively identified adult patients from the ACS TQIP dataset with traumatic SDH, MLS >5 mm, and ED disposition to either the ICU or OR. We defined patient phenotypes using latent class analysis (LCA) and investigated associations between ED disposition and outcomes (inpatient mortality, favorable discharge) using risk-adjusted hierarchical logistic regression. We tested for interaction between patient phenotype and ED disposition and repeated these analyses among patients undergoing an ICU stay ≥1 day and cranial surgery.

Results: Among 9582 patients, 29% (N = 2794) were triaged to the OR. Two LCA-informed phenotypes emerged: class 1 (older-mild injury) and class 2 (younger-severe injury). There was an interaction between ED disposition and patient phenotype, such that younger-severe patients had lower mortality with OR triage (P < 0.001). In the subgroup of 4573 patients (48%) with ≥1 day of ICU stay who underwent cranial surgery, there was a significant interaction between OR triage and the older-mild phenotype indicating increased mortality (P = 0.003).

Conclusions: For traumatic SDH with MLS >5 mm, triage the OR was associated with improved outcomes only among younger, severely-injured patients, while older, mildly-injured patients may benefit from early ICU stabilization. These findings support phenotype-guided ED triage strategies to optimize outcomes.

item.title: J Emerg Med: A Novel Governance Model for Real-Time Clinical Decision-Making in Viral Hemorrhagic Fever Outbreaks: Ethiopia's 2025 Marburg Virus Disease Response
item.description:
Background: In November 2025, Ethiopia declared its first Marburg Virus Disease outbreak. With no licensed vaccines or specific therapeutics, the Ministry of Health established a novel dual-advisory governance structure for case management.

Objectives: This case study examines the development, implementation, and associated outcomes of Ethiopia's dual-advisory governance model during the 2025 Marburg outbreak.

Methods: We conducted a qualitative case study using thematic synthesis of official government documents, meeting minutes, and clinical logs from November 13, 2025, to January 26, 2026. The Ministry of Health granted access; all patient data were anonymized.

Results: The dual-advisory model comprised two parallel bodies: a strategic Technical Working Group for national guideline development, and a tactical National Advisory Team providing daily consultation to frontline clinicians. A ``morning meeting'' mechanism enabled bidirectional communication. During the response, Remdesivir was deployed within 6 days (278 post-exposure prophylaxis [PEP] courses, 10 treatment courses); monoclonal antibody MBP091 was operationalized within 8 days. The outbreak resulted in 14 confirmed cases, five survivors, and three healthcare worker infections (two deceased).

Conclusions: Ethiopia's dual-advisory governance model demonstrated the ability to bridge strategic planning and tactical clinical action. The separation of functions, institutionalized daily communication, and links to resource mobilization represent potentially transferable principles for outbreak governance. However, as a descriptive case study, observed outcomes cannot be attributed to the model, and further evaluation is needed.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Community-based health navigation to reduce drug-related harms in rural settings: A pooled analysis of two intervention trials
item.description:
Background: People who use drugs in rural communities face barriers to accessing services that reduce overdose and infectious disease risk. Community-based navigation may help bridge these gaps, but limited evidence exists to support its effectiveness in real-world rural settings. This study aimed to estimate the effect of two adapted prevention navigation interventions on substance use outcomes among people who use drugs from rural communities.

Methods: We conducted a pooled analysis of two pragmatic trials using harmonized measures, one cluster-randomized trial and one quasi-experimental trial. Participants were adults who use opioids and/or stimulants, recruited through syringe service programs, jails, or pretrial service agencies. The intervention was an adaptation of Project START, delivered by trained prevention navigators; the comparator was usual care, consisting of standard harm reduction and referral services. The primary outcome was change in past 30-day opioid use between baseline and three-month follow-up. Secondary outcomes included days of stimulant use and self-identified drug of choice. Regression models were adjusted for age, gender, and race/ethnicity.

Results: Among 289 individuals with complete outcome data, intervention participants reported a greater reduction in opioid use compared with controls (pooled mean difference: -2.98 days; 95% CI: -5.53, -0.42). Changes in stimulant use and use of drug of choice were not statistically significant but trended in the same direction.

Conclusions: An adapted community-based prevention navigation intervention delivered by trained navigators was associated with a modest but significant reduction in past 30-day opioid use among people who use drugs in rural communities, compared with usual care.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Chatbot-delivered alcohol screening and brief intervention for working-age adults: A proof-of-concept randomised waitlist-controlled trial
item.description:
Background: This study adapted a web-based chatbot to deliver screening and brief intervention (SBI) and assessed its usability, engagement, and preliminary between-group estimates for alcohol-related outcomes.

Methods: This randomised waitlist-controlled trial recruited 304 community-dwelling working-age adults with an Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-C (AUDIT-C) score ≥ 3 in Hong Kong from 15 October 2024-12 May 2025 and randomised 1:1 to the intervention group (IG; n = 152) or waitlist control group (WL; n = 152). Both groups received standardised alcohol brief intervention (ABI) at baseline. The IG received web-based chatbot-delivered SBI immediately, while WL received it after the 4-week follow-up. The primary outcome was weekly alcohol consumption (grams/week) at 4-week follow-up. Secondary outcomes included AUDIT score, chatbot engagement (defined as having read the chatbot messages and interacted with the chatbot more than once during the intervention period, verified by system log files), and 15-item Bot Usability Scale [BUS]. To evaluate cost-effectiveness and scalability, an economic evaluation of intervention-related costs and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) estimated from EQ-5D-5L utility scores were calculated.

Results: By intention-to-treat analysis, the adjusted between-group difference in weekly alcohol consumption was -10.2g/week (95% CI: -33.8-13.4; P = 0.40) and AUDIT score was b = -2.6 (95% CI: -4.6-1.4; P = 0.46) at 4 weeks. Chatbot process indicators showed satisfactory use, with an engagement rate of 56.2% (171/304), a mean BUS score of 56.8/75 (SD 7.8), and overall satisfaction of 7.8/10. The mean intervention-related cost was HKD 489.5 (USD 62.9) per participant, and EQ-5D-5L utility scores increased from 0.870 to 0.909 in the IG and from 0.860 to 0.876 in the WL.

Conclusions: The chatbot-delivered SBI showed satisfactory usability and moderate engagement, supporting its feasibility and acceptability. This trial did not show an incremental effect on alcohol consumption over the standardised ABI received by both groups. Future trial with longer follow-up and a control condition that better isolates the chatbot component is warranted.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Impact of drug scheduling on detection of bromazolam in the unregulated opioid supply: An interrupted time series analysis
item.description:
Background: Adulteration of unregulated opioids with benzodiazepines is a major public health concern. National and international bodies maintain statutes and conventions regulating novel psychoactive substances based on harm potential, yet evidence on the impacts of scheduling substances under these policy instruments remains limited.

Methods: We analysed 43,760 samples tested at 142 drug checking sites in British Columbia (BC) (March 2022-February 2026). Using interrupted time-series (ITS) analysis, we assessed changes in bromazolam detection in opioids following three interventions: when the World Health Organization (WHO) recommended bromazolam be scheduled by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime's Commission on Narcotic Drugs (UNODC/CND) (October 2023); when the People's Republic of China (PRC) scheduled bromazolam domestically (July 2024); when UNODC/CND scheduling entered force (December 2024).

Results: Bromazolam emerged in expected opioid samples in March 2022. In ITS analyses, WHO's scheduling recommendation was associated with a significant slope decrease in bromazolam detection (-0.79 %age points [pp]; 95%confidence interval [CI]:-1.02,-0.56), PRC's ban was associated with a significant step increase (5.44pp; 95%CI:2.46,8.04), and accelerated slope decrease (-0.55pp; 95%CI:-1.00,-0.10). The final absolute trend suggests bromazolam detection stabilised at a lower level than the pre-scheduling period. First-differenced correlation demonstrated significant biweekly substitution of bromazolam with desalkylgidazepm (ρ = -0.22,p = 0.03).

Discussion: Findings suggest unregulated drug manufacturers may be responsive to regulatory signals through anticipatory shifts and analogue substitution. Rather than eliminating benzodiazepine prevalence, results suggest scheduling catalysed market fragmentation, underscoring the need for comprehensive public health interventions to mitigate risks from an increasingly unstable unregulated drug supply.

item.title: Drug Alcohol Depend: Effects of remifentanil/ketamine mixtures in rats responding under a choice procedure
item.description:
Background: Despite a number of adverse effects, opioids continue to be the gold standard treatment for moderate to severe pain. One potential way to treat pain while avoiding or reducing adverse effects is to combine opioids with other non-opioid analgesic drugs, thereby decreasing the dose of opioid needed. Our laboratory previously reported that mixing morphine with the N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonist ketamine produced additive or greater than additive effects antinociceptive effects in rats.

Objective: The purpose of the present experiment was to determine how ketamine interacts with the opioid agonist remifentanil for reinforcing effects.

Methods: This experiment employed an operant choice paradigm, giving rats a concurrent choice between a food pellet alone or a food pellet plus an intravenous infusion. In one group of rats, the effects of remifentanil alone and ketamine alone were determined and compared to saline. In a second group of rats, the effects of remifentanil/ketamine mixtures were determined and compared to saline.

Results: All rats were indifferent to a pellet versus saline + a pellet. When available alone, remifentanil had reinforcing effects, while ketamine had punishing effects. Remifentanil/ketamine mixtures, across a range of doses, had no significant difference from saline. These results demonstrate that ketamine fails to enhance, and might even attenuate, reinforcing effects of remifentanil.

Conclusion: Overall, this adds to the evidence in the literature that combining opioids with non-opioids is a useful strategy for relieving pain while minimizing adverse effects.

item.title: J Addict Med: Medical Cannabis and Opioid Prescription Discontinuation Among Chronic Pain Patients on Long-term Opioid Therapy
item.description:
Objectives: To examine the association between medical cannabis use and discontinuation of prescription opioids among patients with chronic pain receiving long-term opioid therapy, overall, by time, and opioid dosage.

Methods: We used New York State Medical Cannabis and Prescription Monitoring Program data (2017-2019), including 8358 patients on long-term opioid therapy, who also received medical cannabis for chronic pain. Patients were followed for 90 days and were classified as "medical cannabis patients" if they received medical cannabis for >30 days and "no-medical cannabis" if they received 30 days or less. Prescription opioid discontinuation was defined as a break in opioid prescriptions of 45 days or longer. Multivariate time-to-event models [stratified by baseline morphine milligram equivalent (MME)] were used.

Results: The medical cannabis group included 4892 patients, and the no-medical cannabis group included 3466 patients. Overall, opioid prescription discontinuation was 2 times higher among those using medical cannabis (15.5%), compared with the no-medical cannabis group (7.6%) (P<0.001). Among patients with a baseline MME <50, opioid discontinuation was faster in the first 30 days of the follow-up period, with an adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) of 2.87 (95% CI: 2.22-3.70) and reduced to 1.81 (95% CI: 1.43-2.29) after 30 days. For patients with a baseline MME 50-<90, the aHR was 3.13 (95% CI: 2.09-4.68) throughout follow-up. No significant associations were found among patients with a baseline MME ≥90.

Conclusions: Patients receiving medical cannabis were more likely to discontinue prescription opioids, which may lower morbidity and mortality risks associated with long-term opioid therapy or abrupt discontinuation of opioid prescriptions.

item.title: N Engl J Med: In Vitro Fertilization or Intrauterine Insemination in Unexplained Infertility
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
Background: Although international guidelines recommend intrauterine insemination (IUI) with ovarian stimulation as first-line treatment for unexplained infertility, evidence from comparisons of this method with in vitro fertilization (IVF) is limited.

Methods: We conducted a sequential, multicenter, randomized, controlled trial involving couples with unexplained infertility. Stage 1 was a noninferiority comparison between IUI with ovarian stimulation (up to four cycles) and IVF (one complete cycle, with transfer of all embryos). After 7 months, couples without live birth or ongoing pregnancy could proceed to stage 2: couples in the IUI group could undergo up to two IVF cycles, and those in the IVF group could undergo one further IVF cycle. The primary outcome was the cumulative live-birth rate resulting from stage 1. Couples who were in stage 1 during lockdowns due to coronavirus disease 2019 were omitted from the analysis of the primary outcome. A secondary outcome was the cumulative live-birth rate resulting from stages 1 and 2. Live births were included in analyses if day 1 of the treatment cycle that led to pregnancy or day 1 of the last menstrual period before conception occurred within 7 months (stage 1) or 20 months (stage 2) after randomization. The noninferiority margin for the primary outcome was a between-group difference of 10 percentage points.

Results: A total of 737 couples underwent randomization: 365 couples were assigned to undergo IUI with ovarian stimulation before IVF, and 372 were assigned to undergo first-line IVF (1 couple in the IVF group withdrew consent for the use of data). The primary-outcome analysis included 585 couples (288 in the IUI group and 297 in the IVF group). The cumulative live-birth rate from stage 1 was 31% (89 births among 288 couples) with IUI with ovarian stimulation and 55% (164 births among 297 couples) with IVF (adjusted risk difference, -24 percentage points; 95% confidence interval [CI], -31 to -16). The cumulative live-birth rate from stages 1 and 2 among all the couples who had undergone randomization and provided consent was 70% (257 births among 365 couples) and 71% (265 births among 371 couples), respectively (adjusted risk difference, 0 percentage points; 99% CI, -9 to 8). Overall, serious adverse events occurred in 6 couples in the IUI group and in 14 couples in the IVF group; most serious adverse events were related to oocyte retrieval or hyperstimulation.

Conclusions: In couples with unexplained infertility, treatment with four cycles of IUI with ovarian stimulation was not noninferior to treatment with one complete cycle of IVF with respect to the cumulative live-birth rate. item.title: N Engl J Med: Gram-Negative Bacterial Resistance
item.category: The New England journal of medicine
item.description:
The rapid worldwide spread of antimicrobial resistance among gram-negative bacteria is driven by a complex interplay of human, environmental, and health care-associated factors and accelerated by mobile genetic elements that facilitate the dissemination of resistance genes. Resistance in gram-negative bacteria arises primarily through reduced drug entry, active drug efflux, modification of antibiotic targets, and enzymatic drug inactivation, most notably through β-lactamase production. Clinically important resistant pathogens include extended-spectrum β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales, carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas aeruginosa with difficult-to-treat resistance, and carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii. Limited access to effective antibiotics and the continued emergence of resistance to available agents pose substantial challenges to the management of these infections. Appropriate management requires timely and accurate diagnostics, targeted use of newer β-lactam agents, effective source control, and judicious selection of treatment durations.

item.title: JAMA: Left Bundle-Branch Area Pacing vs Right Ventricular Pacing for Atrioventricular Block and Preserved Left Ventricular Function: The LEAP-Block Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: For patients with atrioventricular block requiring high-burden ventricular pacing, the optimal pacing strategy to reduce heart failure (HF) and all-cause mortality remains uncertain. Robust comparative evidence on the clinical outcomes of left bundle-branch area pacing (LBBAP) vs right ventricular pacing (RVP) in this population is needed.

Objective: To compare 24-month clinical outcomes of LBBAP vs RVP in patients with atrioventricular block and preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF; ≥50%).

Design, setting, and participants: The LEAP-Block study was a prospective, multicenter, randomized, controlled, superiority trial conducted across 14 Chinese hospitals from January 2021 to August 2025, with last follow-up on June 3, 2025. Of 551 patients with LVEF 50% or greater requiring ventricular pacing who underwent eligibility assessment, 499 with anticipated ventricular pacing greater than 40% were randomized.

Interventions: Patients were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to LBBAP (n = 249) or RVP (n = 250).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary end point was a composite of all-cause death, HF events, or upgrade to biventricular pacing at 24 months. Secondary end points included pacing-induced cardiomyopathy and device-related complications.

Results: The primary analysis included 482 patients (LBBAP, n = 242; RVP, n = 240; mean age, 67 years; 46% female). Acute procedure success was comparable between the 2 groups (LBBAP, 237/242 [97.9%] vs RVP, 239/240 [99.6%]; P = .22), with left bundle-branch capture confirmed in 188 of 236 patients (79.7%). LBBAP significantly reduced the primary end point vs RVP (2.4% vs 12.5%, respectively; absolute risk difference, -10.1% [95% CI, -16.8% to -3.4%]; P = .003). Among secondary outcomes, the LBBAP group had fewer HF events (3.4% vs 11.3%; -7.9% [95% CI, -13.0% to -2.8%]). The 24-month Kaplan-Meier estimated cumulative incidence of the primary end point was 5.0% for LBBAP vs 13.2% for RVP (hazard ratio, 0.37 [95% CI, 0.19 to 0.73]; P = .004). item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Exercise Training During Neoadjuvant Treatment for Gastroesophageal Cancer and Tumor Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Physical deterioration and disease progression during neoadjuvant treatment can preclude tumor surgery in patients with gastroesophageal cancer. Whether preoperative exercise training can increase the probability of undergoing tumor surgery remains unknown.

Objective: To compare exercise training with usual care on the likelihood of not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent after neoadjuvant treatment for gastroesophageal cancer.

Design, setting, and participants: PRESET-RCT was a single-blinded, parallel-group, 2-arm, superiority randomized clinical trial. Patients with gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma scheduled to undergo treatment with curative intent, including neoadjuvant treatment, and with no contraindication to exercise training were eligible. Participants were enrolled at University Hospital Copenhagen, Rigshospitalet, Copenhagen, Denmark, from August 16, 2018, to September 23, 2022, with final follow-up on October 22, 2024. Data analysis was performed from March 2023 to May 2025.

Intervention: The participants were randomized 1:1 to preoperative exercise training from diagnosis until tumor surgery or control. The intervention consisted of twice-weekly concurrent aerobic exercise and resistance training.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was not undergoing tumor surgery with curative intent. The secondary outcomes were treatment tolerance and overall survival.

Results: In total, 207 participants (73.7%) were randomized and 202 were included in the modified intention-to-treat analyses (mean [SD] age, 65.3 [8.5] years; 161 [78.9%] male; 170 [83.3%] with gastroesophageal junction cancer), with 101 randomized to each group. In the exercise group, 10 (9.9%) did not undergo tumor surgery with curative intent compared with 8 (7.9%) in the control group (odds ratio, 1.28; 95% CI, 0.48-3.38; P = .62). There were no between-group differences in permanent discontinuation of neoadjuvant treatment (odds ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.38-1.72) or postoperative complications (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.61-2.20). The overall survival rates at 3 years for the exercise and control group were 51.0% and 65.0%, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.58; 95% CI, 1.02-2.45).

Conclusion and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial, preoperative exercise training did not increase the likelihood of undergoing tumor surgery for patients with gastroesophageal cancer. The findings do not support the use of exercise training during neoadjuvant treatment to improve surgical outcomes, and further research is needed to determine its effects on long-term outcomes.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Organ Preservation With Watch and Wait in Patients With Rectal Cancer
item.description:
Importance: With growing evidence and evolving guidelines, organ preservation with watch and wait for stage II to III rectal cancer after neoadjuvant therapy is increasingly implemented. However, the true frequency of watch-and-wait use is unknown.

Objective: To estimate rates of intentional organ preservation with watch and wait by evaluating secular trends across age groups.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study used data from the National Cancer Database (NCDB), with analyses conducted in September 2025. Patients with stage II to III rectal cancer diagnosed between 2006 and 2023 who received neoadjuvant chemoradiation in Commission on Cancer-accredited hospitals participating in the NCDB across the US were included.

Exposure: Age, year of diagnosis, and treatment strategy (proctectomy vs nonsurgical management).

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome consisted of watch-and-wait rates, defined as excess nonsurgical management greater than baseline. To account for nonsurgical management unrelated to the decision for watch and wait, joinpoint regression estimated baseline rates of nonsurgical management and annual percentage changes. A secondary analysis examined associations of age and year with watch-and-wait rates using multivariable logistic regression.

Results: Among 101 001 patients with rectal cancer (median [IQR] age, 60 [51-69] years; 37 957 female [37.58%]), 84 324 underwent surgery and 16 677 did not. Baseline rates of nonsurgical management remained stable through 2014. Joinpoints occurred in 2014 and 2019, with annual percentage changes of -0.45% (95% CI, -2.26% to 0.78%; P = .42) in 2006 to 2014, 9.83% (95% CI, 4.66% to 13.73%; P = .001) in 2015 to 2018, and 21.71% (95% CI, 17.74% to 29.57%; P < .001) in 2019 to 2023. Baseline nonsurgical management increased with age, from 1331 of 19 785 patients younger than 50 years (6.73%) to 1748 of 6210 patients aged 80 years and older (28.15%). Earlier adoption occurred in older patients; the group aged 80 years and older surpassed 5-percentage point excess watch and wait by 2015 (33.78% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [5.63-percentage point excess]) and 10% by 2017 (39.56% annual rate vs 28.15% baseline rate [11.41-percentage point excess]), compared with 2019 (12.88% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [6.15-percentage point excess]) and 2021 (20.75% annual rate vs 6.73% baseline rate [14.02%] excess) in patients younger than 50 years. Overall, watch and wait increased from 140 of 6101 patients (2.30%) in 2015 to 2068 of 6280 patients (32.94%) in 2023. Increasing year (odds ratio for 2023 vs 2006, 6.23; 95% CI, 5.48 to 7.09) and older age (odds ratio for ages ≥80 vs <50 years, 4.25; 95% CI, 3.98 to 4.54) were independently associated with nonsurgical management (both P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, watch-and-wait rates increased across all age groups, with a marked acceleration after 2019 suggesting evidence-concordant adoption of the watch-and-wait approach. This underscores the need for careful patient selection, accurate clinical response assessment, and rigorous surveillance monitoring to ensure safe oncologic outcomes.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Bias-Adjusted Prevalence of Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Among Deceased National Football League Players
item.description:
Importance: The majority of knowledge regarding chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in National Football League (NFL) players is derived from autopsy-based studies on voluntarily donated brains. Because these cohorts are highly vulnerable to selection bias (specifically registry bias), population-level prevalence of CTE among former NFL players is unknown, limiting understanding of the impact of this disease.

Objective: To estimate the selection-bias adjusted prevalence of CTE neuropathology in deceased NFL players.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cross-sectional study used Understanding Neurologic Injury and Traumatic Encephalopathy (UNITE) brain bank data combined with National Death Index records on former NFL players. Both brain donor and nondonor NFL players who died between January 2008 and December 2023 were included. Data were analyzed from November 2025 to April 2026.

Exposure: Playing in at least 1 regular or postseason NFL game.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcomes of this study were bias-adjusted prevalence of CTE neuropathology and all-cause dementia among the target population, both of which were measured in donors prior to this study. A cognitive symptom-related brain donation selection ratio (probability of donation given CTE divided by the probability of donation given no CTE) was estimated using Poisson regression and was applied to adjust donor-observed prevalence of CTE neuropathology at death and all-cause dementia during life. The prevalence estimates were adjusted for bias using the estimated selection ratio.

Results: The cohort consisted of 2362 deceased former NFL players (mean [SD] years played, 5.1 [3.9]; 971 [41.1%] aged ≥80 years at death), of whom 396 were brain donors and 1966 were nondonors. Of 387 donors, 362 (93.5%) had CTE. The median selection ratio was 4.97 (95% CI, 4.72-5.26). Bias-adjusted population prevalence of CTE at death was 74.5% (95% CI, 69.6%-78.3%), with a conservative lower-bound analysis estimating 63.7% (57.2%-68.9%). Bias-adjusted population prevalence of all-cause dementia history during life was 27.2% (95% CI, 22.6%-31.6%).

Conclusions and relevance: The findings of this cross-sectional study suggest that selection bias materially inflates donor-based prevalence estimates but is unlikely to fully explain the high burden of CTE neuropathology among this population. Further research is required to understand the clinical impact of this disease.

item.title: JAMA Netw Open: Effectiveness of the mRNA-1345 Vaccine Against Respiratory Syncytial Virus in US Veterans
item.description:
Importance: In clinical trials, the messenger RNA (mRNA)-1345 vaccine provided protection against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) illness. Data on mRNA-1345 effectiveness in broader patient populations are needed.

Objective: To estimate the effectiveness of mRNA-1345 vaccination during a single respiratory illness season.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used a target trial emulation framework to assess veterans 50 years and older receiving care in the Veterans Health Administration. Eligible vaccine recipients were matched with up to 4 unvaccinated individuals in 4 monthly, nested, sequential trials from October 1, 2025, to January 31, 2026. Outcomes were ascertained through May 31, 2026, or 24 weeks.

Exposure: A single dose of mRNA-1345 RSV vaccine vs no RSV vaccination.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was any positive RSV test result from day 14 after the matched index date. Secondary outcomes included RSV-associated emergency department (ED) or urgent care (UC) encounters and RSV-associated hospitalizations. Vaccine effectiveness was estimated as 100 × (1 - risk ratio). A sensitivity analysis comparing veterans who received same-day mRNA-1345 and influenza vaccination to influenza vaccination alone (active comparator arm) was performed to explore potential bias from differences in health care-seeking behavior and outcome ascertainment between comparator groups.

Results: A total of 74 926 vaccinated veterans were matched to 286 425 unique control individuals, weighted to represent 74 926 individuals, for a total of 149 852 study participants (median [IQR] age, 73.0 [63.3-78.6] years; 136 756 [91.3%] male). During a median (IQR) follow-up of 160 (130-168) days, estimated vaccine effectiveness was 60.3% (95% CI, 49.0%-70.4%) against any documented infection, 60.2% (95% CI, 47.2%-71.5%) against RSV-associated ED or UC encounters, and 81.8% (95% CI, 58.1%-99.9%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations. Estimated effectiveness against documented infections decreased with increasing age, from 82.9% (95% CI, 64.0%-96.7%) in the 50- to 59-year age group to 28.6% (95% CI, -12.0% to 60.4%) in the 80-year or older age group. With an active comparator arm, estimated effectiveness was 67.1% (95% CI, 48.9%-82.6%) against documented RSV infections, 69.5% (95% CI, 49.7%-85.4%) against RSV-associated ED and UC encounters, and 86.9% (95% CI, 56.5%-100.0%) against RSV-associated hospitalizations.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study using a target trial emulation of mRNA-1345 vaccine effectiveness during 24 weeks, vaccination was associated with protection against RSV illness and associated health care use in adults 50 years and older. Comparative effectiveness studies are needed to determine the relative benefits of available RSV vaccine products.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Fatal Opioid-Like Toxidrome Associated With a 7-Hydroxymitragynine Kratom Product
item.description:
Kratom (Mitragyna speciosa) use has increased in the United States, with the market shifting from traditional leaf preparations to concentrated products containing concentrated or chemically processed alkaloids such as 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-HMG) and mitragynine pseudoindoxyl. These formulations may deliver supraphysiologic opioid-receptor agonist doses with poorly characterized toxicity. A 42-year-old man was found dead at home after reportedly ingesting 3 tablets of a commercial "7-HMG" product and several beers. Postmortem examination revealed purge fluid at the mouth and nose, severe bilateral pulmonary edema, distended bladder, and no evidence of trauma or injection drug use. Quantitative analysis of the remaining tablet showed 29 mg 7-HMG and 0.58 mg mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, with minimal mitragynine. Postmortem blood contained 37.3 ng/mL 7-HMG and 76 ng/mL mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, whereas gabapentin and other medications were present at subtherapeutic concentrations. Compared with an estimated 1 to 4.5 mg 7-HMG in a typical high dose of dried kratom leaf powder, this ingestion delivered approximately 87 mg 7-HMG (19-fold to 87-fold greater 7-HMG exposure than a high-dose botanical leaf preparation). Given the high μ-opioid receptor activity of 7-HMG and its in vivo conversion to the even more potent opioid agonist mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, the postmortem findings are most consistent with a fatal opioid-like toxidrome associated with exposure to concentrated kratom alkaloids. This case illustrates the emerging risk posed by new kratom-branded products containing purified or chemically enriched alkaloids at doses far exceeding traditional preparations.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Associations Between Diagnostic Blood-Based Biomarkers and Neuroimaging Findings in Mild Traumatic Brain Injury
item.description:
Study objective: Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) is a prevalent and resource-intensive injury in the emergency department (ED). The blood-based biomarkers glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) and ubiquitin c-terminal hydrolase L1 (UCH-L1) have demonstrated diagnostic potential for acute structural brain injury. Our objective was to clinically validate a US Food and Drug Administration-approved plasma test to aid in the identification of intracranial injury in patients with mTBI presenting to the ED and assess its integration with existing protocols.

Methods: This single-center validation study enrolled 104 adult patients with suspected mTBI undergoing head computed tomography (CT) for evaluation between October 2023 and June 2024 at a Level I trauma center. Peripheral blood draw was completed within 12 hours postinjury and processed at the hospital clinical laboratory. Sensitivity, specificity, and predictive values for the test were calculated and compared with a standard clinical decision rule (Canadian Head CT Rule). ED length of stay and diagnostic turnaround times were examined.

Results: Within the cohort (n=104), 83 patients had elevated biomarker levels (GFAP >30 pg/mL or UCH-L1 >360 pg/mL), and 11 patients had intracranial injury identified on CT. The combination plasma test demonstrated high sensitivity (0.91 [95% confidence interval {CI} 0.59 to 1.00]) but low specificity (0.22 [95% CI 0.14 to 0.31]) for predicting intracranial injury on CT with low positive predictive value (0.12 [95% CI 0.06 to 0.21]) and high negative predictive value (0.95 [95% CI 0.76 to 1.00]). These findings are consistent with prior studies (pooled sensitivity 0.97 [95% CI 0.95 to 0.98]; specificity 0.28 [95% CI 0.23 to 0.34]). False-positive cases (78%) were older than true-negative cases (median 72 years [interquartile range (IQR) 54 to 83] versus 58.5 years [IQR 38.25 to 66]). Median turnaround time for the GFAP/UCH-L1 test was 2 hours faster than head CT (1.09 hours [IQR 0.87 to 1.65] versus 3.28 hours [IQR 2.37 to 4.70]).

Conclusions: Blood biomarkers for mTBI have potential as an initial rule-out tool for intracranial injury prior to obtaining CT imaging; however, large multicenter studies are needed to clarify its impact on ED resource utilization, length of stay, and acute and long-term costs and benefits to patients and health care systems.

item.title: Ann Emerg Med: Ambient Artificial Intelligence Scribe Use and Objective Documentation Effort Among Emergency Physicians
item.description:
Study objective: Ambient artificial intelligence (AI) scribes ("AI scribes") are purported to reduce emergency department (ED) documentation burden, but ED evidence is largely single-site, uncontrolled, or self-reported, with exposure inferred rather than measured. We evaluated AI scribe use among attending emergency physicians across a multisite network, with exposure and outcomes read directly from the electronic health record.

Methods: Across 20 EDs (3 academic and 17 community), AI scribe use was flagged per note from the patient consent statement within the ED note. Analyses were restricted to attending physicians and, to isolate the physician's own documentation, excluded teaching encounters and attestation notes identified from standardized attestation text. Endpoints, computed over the mature-adoption window (December 2025 onward, when Epic audit-log data are retained), were active time in the note (primary), note length, note-start time, completion lag, and 72-hour ED return. Within-physician models (physician and calendar-month fixed effects, clustered by physician) compared each adopter's AI-scribed notes with their own unassisted notes, adjusting only for pre-exposure case mix.

Results: Among 275 attending physicians, 31% of encounters were AI-scribed. Physicians spent less active time in AI-scribed notes (median 10.0 versus 12.5 min-2.4 minutes after adjustment), started them about 15 minutes later (median 31 versus 17 minutes after first seeing the patient, and produced notes about 14% longer [median 5,220 versus 4,468 characters; within-physician +629 characters]). Note completion was not delayed (-6 minutes), and 72-hour ED return was not increased (-0.8 percentage point; 95% confidence interval -1.5 to -0.1).

Conclusion: Among emergency physicians, AI scribe use was associated with less active time in the note, deferred note-start, and longer notes, without delaying completion or increasing short-term returns, with effect sizes consistent with ambulatory randomized data.

Study objective: We aimed to describe trainee performance and tracheal intubation outcomes in academic pediatric emergency departments.

Methods: We conducted a multicenter retrospective observational study of intubations performed between January 2021 and December 2023, using data from the National Emergency Airway Registry for Pediatric Emergency Medicine. Eligible encounters included children who underwent intubation with the first-attempt proceduralist identified as an emergency medicine resident, a pediatric resident, or a pediatric emergency medicine (PEM) fellow.
